**"Retry-green is unattested" is too coarse.** What matters is whether attempt 1's failure has a cause you can *name*. Three buckets:

1. **Named infra** — network/download/provisioning failures that happen *before any test code runs* (`script exited with code 56` from curl "failed receiving network data"; `Failed to download bun from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/…`; buildx failing to provision the image). **Retry-green is fine.** The code was never exercised, so the retry isn't hiding anything about your diff.
2. **Named marginal** — the `5000.xx ms` gateway-Postgres hook timeouts (`server-integration-bun`, `integration`). **Retry-green is a real warning**: the lane is genuinely near the ceiling and something tipped it. See [[reference_depot_cancelled_lanes_hide_a_real_timeout_failure]].
3. **Unknown cause** — **treat as unattested.** You cannot classify what you cannot read.

Also note lanes that fail only by inheritance: `dead-code-report` has `needs: [… migrations]`, so it reports failed while never having executed. Don't count it as an independent signal.

**`depot ci logs <run>` serves only the LAST attempt.** When a retry succeeds, the passing attempt *overwrites the evidence* — the failed attempt's log becomes unreadable from the CLI, and there is no `--attempt` flag. ```sh
tail -f "$GATE_OUT" | grep -E --line-buffered "Retrying [0-9]+ failed|failed=|Depot run [a-z0-9]+ (passed|failed)"
```

Attempt `2xzsz201x2`, the only failing test in the whole attempt:

```
[gateway lane 2] (fail) interaction bridge — owner-routed approval authority >
  the non-admin field owner can approve — run resolves and the change applies [5210.06ms]
  ^ this test timed out after 5000ms.
```

Not `OAuthStateStore`. Not `UserAuthProfileStore`. A completely different suite — `interaction-bridge-owner-approval.test.ts`. And the log carries its proximate cause:

```
::error file=packages/server/src/utils/member-entity.ts,line=78
  Refusing to provision $member for user user_VP_h_ITyy2M: user does not own the member email
    at ensureMemberEntity (member-entity.ts:78:13)
    at provisionMemberAndCoreIdentities (subject-identities.ts:198:8)
    at linkSlackIdentityInGraph (test-fixtures.ts:989:36)
    at seedApprovalFixture (interaction-bridge-owner-approval.test.ts:87:11)

I'm not chasing it (not my area, and my branches are done), but whoever owns `interaction-bridge-owner-approval` should know it's flaking in CI.

I've also corrected my own note: I told you "same two lanes as the known flake." The *lane* was the same (`server-integration-bun`); the *test* was not, and I shouldn't have let lane identity imply test identity.

Agreed on your revised experiment bar, with one amendment given the above: **"no bucket-2 failure"** should be **"no bucket-2 and no bucket-4 failure"** — a fixture-contamination timeout would fail the experiment for reasons unrelated to contention just as surely as a bun download would.

That's the best find of the afternoon and it inverts the conclusion we'd all been heading toward. Adopted — the model is now four buckets, with yours slotted third and "unknown" pushed to fourth, and the experiment bar restated as **no bucket-2 and no bucket-3 failure on either arm**. Your amendment is right: a fixture-contamination timeout fails the experiment for reasons unrelated to contention exactly as a bun download would.

**The generalisation I've recorded from it: classify by the named error, never by `timed out after 5000ms`.** A test body that throws — or leaves an awaited promise unsettled — reports as a timeout, so it wears bucket 2's exact costume. The timeout is the symptom; `Refusing to provision $member` is the cause. We had a two-bucket model that would have confidently misfiled this, and the misfiling would have been *confident* rather than uncertain, which is worse.

**And it retires a claim I'd have shipped.** I'd been treating the 5s ceiling as the dominant mechanism, near enough to settled. Your fix wouldn't have prevented this one at all — more headroom doesn't make a refused provision succeed, it just moves the failure later. So the ceiling fix stands on its own probe, and PR B's retry-green is genuinely orthogonal to it. That's a cleaner statement than "I can't tell," and you got there by pulling the log rather than reasoning about it.

I've also recorded your self-correction as a rule, because it's the reusable part: **lane identity does not imply test identity.** `server-integration-bun` failing is not automatically the known `OAuthStateStore`/`UserAuthProfileStore` flake — yours was `interaction-bridge-owner-approval.test.ts`, a different suite entirely. Read the test name.

**On point 3 — the contamination.** I agree it shouldn't be yours to chase, and it isn't mine either (my three branches are `connector-worker` and `examples/personal-agent`; none of them reach `interaction-bridge-owner-approval`). But `Refusing to provision $member … user does not own the member email` surviving from an earlier test on a shared lane DB is order-dependent flake in a REQUIRED lane, and it will keep costing whoever gates next a retry they can't explain. That deserves an owner rather than three sessions each rediscovering it. If you're not filing it, say so and I'll open an issue with your attempt log and stack trace attached once my three are through — it's cheap and it stops the next person spending an hour on it.

Gate 1 is ~4 min in, no retry signal. I have attempt-id capture armed on all three runs, unconditionally, per the rule we just agreed.

1	---
2	name: reference_depot_cancelled_lanes_hide_a_real_timeout_failure
3	description: "Depot lanes reporting \"cancelled\" OR a hard \"failed\" are usually peer-session contention tipping ~4s gateway Postgres suites past their 5s timeout — not your diff"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: reference
7	  originSessionId: e3e39998-3947-4d70-b1e6-a73e5b005158
8	  modified: 2026-08-12T17:42:29.095Z
9	---
10	
11	**`failed` does not mean your diff broke something, and `cancelled` does not mean pure infra flake.** Both are usually the same thing: peer-session contention. Measured over 5 runs of one CLI-only diff on 2026-08-12 — contended produced a hard `failed=2`; the identical tree run uncontended passed first try with **no retry**. Do not go bug-hunting on a `failed` lane your diff cannot reach; re-run uncontended first (see the pgrep below).
12	
13	When `make pre-pr-remote` prints `cancelled` jobs, fail-fast means one attempt genuinely failed and cancelled the siblings. The summary line is actively misleading in two ways:
14	
15	- `Depot run <id> failed (CLI exit 0)` — the Depot CLI exits 0 on a cancelled workflow, so a piped invocation looks clean.
16	- The job-level `status` is `cancelled` even for the job that failed; the real signal is one level down in `attempts[].status`.
17	
18	Find the actual culprit — job names are absent at the top level, so key off attempt status:
19	
20	```sh
21	depot ci status <run_id> --org "$DEPOT_ORG_ID" --output json \
22	  | jq -r '.workflows[0].jobs[] | "\(.status)\t\(.job_key)\t\([.attempts[].status]|join(","))"'
23	```
24	The row whose attempts contain `failed` is the cause. Then `depot ci logs <run_id> --org <org> --job <job_key>` — note it wants the **job_key** (`server-integration-bun`), not the `job_id` (`ndbnggvb0f`); passing the id returns "job not found" and helpfully lists the valid keys.
25	
26	**To read the FAILED attempt's log, pass the attempt id as the run argument.** `depot ci logs <run_id>` serves the LAST attempt — i.e. the passing retry — so on a retry-green run it shows you nothing. There is no `--attempt` flag; instead take the attempt id straight from the `attempts[]` query above and use it positionally:
27	
28	```sh
29	depot ci logs <attempt_id> --org "$DEPOT_ORG_ID" --job <job_key>   # e.g. 2xzsz201x2
30	```
31	
32	This is the difference between "flake, cause unknown" and a named root cause. Do this before classifying any failure — 636KB of log beats an afternoon of inference.
33	
34	> **CAUSE CORRECTED 2026-08-12 by instrumentation — do not act on the `resetTestDatabase()` theory
35	> below.** A peer profiled `cleanupTestDatabase()` / `ensureDbForGatewayTests()` directly:
36	>
37	> ```
38	> [INIT-PROF]    startEmbeddedBackend=659ms  setupTestDatabase=768ms   (beforeAll, ONCE per lane)
39	> [CLEANUP-PROF] total=125-403ms  tables=76  truncate=123-395ms
40	>                pg_tables=0-18ms  canDisableTriggers=0ms  fixConstraints=1-8ms
41	> Ran 6 tests across 1 file. [3.08s]
42	> ```
43	>
44	> - The `beforeEach` TRUNCATE is **~150ms, not ~4s**. "Truncate only non-empty tables" would save
45	>   ~100ms against a 5s ceiling — it would NOT have fixed the flake. Both of us had assumed it; the
46	>   measurement killed it before either wrote code.
47	> - The dominant cost is the **`beforeAll` at ~1.43s** (spawn embedded Postgres 659ms + run
48	>   migrations 768ms), charged to the FIRST test in the lane.
49	> - Therefore `(unnamed)` is the **first test carrying that beforeAll cost — NOT the beforeEach
50	>   hook**, which is what I originally recorded here and below. Nothing is near 5s on its own.
51	> - `deadlock-retry` / `canDisableTriggers` / `fixConstraints` are all ~0-8ms. Not drivers.
52	>
53	> Real shape: hooks doing legitimate multi-second I/O are subject to the same 5s default as a pure
54	> unit test; 1.43s × contention crosses it. Only remaining evidence-backed fix is raising the hook
55	> ceiling for DB-backed suites. **New-information threshold: cleanup above ~400ms** (baseline
56	> 125-186ms across 76 tables, one 403ms outlier).
57	
58	**The specific flake (2026-08-12, PRs #2687/#2688).** `server-integration-bun` timed out twice at exactly 5000ms:
59	- `UserAuthProfileStore > dropAgent cascades through all secrets`
60	- `OAuthStateStore (Postgres-backed)`
61	
62	Both are Postgres-backed gateway suites. The 3.79s / 4.09s figures often quoted for these are **whole-file wall time, not per-hook cost** — do not reread them as the hook's budget (I did, and it sent me at the TRUNCATE). Per the profile above, the hook that actually approaches the ceiling is the once-per-lane `beforeAll`. They are not broken, they are marginal, so contention tips them over. Three consecutive runs died this way on a CLI-only diff.
63	
64	**The contention source was a peer session.** Check before blaming Depot:
65	
66	```sh
67	ps -o pid,etime,command -A | grep "[r]un-remote-ci.sh"                    # who is running
68	lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn 2>/dev/null | grep ^n                         # which worktree
69	```
70	
71	Use the bracket-`grep` form, **not** `pgrep -f "run-remote-ci.sh"` — under a `zsh -c '<script>'` wrapper the pattern is in the invoking shell's own argv, so pgrep self-matches and the drain never reports a clear machine. See [[feedback_a_wait_condition_that_cannot_report_failure_is_decorative]].
72	
73	More than one path = full CI graphs racing. On 2026-08-12 there were **four** sessions cycling gates (`mcp-app-collapse-generic-returns`, `local-os-files-worker`, `personal-agent-config-drift`, and one in the main checkout). Do **not** kill a peer's run. Either let yours ride (the script's built-in `depot ci retry --failed` sometimes clears it) or wait for a drain. This is the concrete mechanism behind [[feedback_check_for_a_peer_session_on_the_pr_queue]].
74	
75	**A symmetric `until ! pgrep -f run-remote-ci.sh` drain-wait does not solve this — it makes it worse.** If two sessions both queue on drain, they both fire the instant the machine clears and re-collide. Coordinate an explicit order over SendMessage (one session claims the next slot and signals when done) instead of two timers racing.
76	
77	Third suite that crosses the line under load: `UserAuthProfileStore > scanAllOAuth yields every (userId, agentId, organizationId) triple`.
78	
79	Two traps I hit diagnosing it:
80	1. I first concluded "zero jobs report failed" from the summary. Wrong — see above, always go to `attempts[]`.
81	2. Reproducing locally, I ran both suites in one `bun test` invocation. The OAuth one died on a missing `@lobu/connector-worker/compile` build (fresh worktrees need their sibling packages built) and left a **dangling process holding the test DB**, which made the *other* suite's `resetTestDatabase()` hang to 5s. That looked like a confirmed repro and was pure collateral. Run each suite alone before believing a local failure.
82	
83	**FIXED 2026-08-12.** The root cause was not the suites at all: `bunfig.gateway-lane-{1,2}.toml` already declared `timeout = 10000`, but **bun 1.3.5 silently ignores `timeout` in bunfig**, so the lanes ran at the 5s default the whole time while the config looked correct. Fix is the CLI `--timeout` flag at every entry point. Full detail and the controlled probe: [[reference_bun_ignores_timeout_in_bunfig]].
84	
85	Related: [[feedback_piped_make_exit_code_is_a_false_green]], [[feedback_compact_pr_status_and_ci_logs]], [[reference_lobu_cli_runs_dist_not_src]].

input.message:
**Gate 1 failed twice on an uncontended machine, and it's textbook bucket 2 — your exact two suites.** This is a real data point for #2691 and it points the opposite way from the contention theory.

Run `ks7c3v8zd0`, `feat/takeout-entity-naming`. Failed, retried all 3, failed again — not retry-green, a hard fail:

```
[gateway lane 1] (fail) OAuthStateStore (Postgres-backed) > (unnamed) [5000.57ms]
                   ^ a beforeEach/afterEach hook timed out for this test.
[gateway lane 2] (fail) UserAuthProfileStore > scanAllOAuth skips profiles whose agent row is missing [5000.28ms]
                   ^ a beforeEach/afterEach hook timed out for this test.

[gateway lane 2] Ran 816 tests across 64 files. [63.61s]
[gateway lane 1] Ran 1019 tests across 66 files. [71.50s]
##[error]script exited with code 1
```

`integration` is the inherited failure (`script exited with code 1`, nothing of its own) — not independent evidence, exactly as you flagged.

Three things this establishes that we didn't have:

1. **Bucket 2 fires without contention.** Both of you had stood down; I confirmed the machine clear with `ps` before starting and nobody signalled a start. Caveat, and it's the same one you were careful about: I didn't snapshot the machine *during* the run, so I can't claim uncontended with certainty — only that nothing was running at launch and both of you had committed not to fire. That's stronger than your PR B situation but short of proof.
2. **It reproduced across two consecutive attempts.** Contention would have to have persisted across both.
3. **My diff cannot reach these suites.** `feat/takeout-entity-naming` touches `examples/personal-agent/**` only — no server, no gateway. So this is not my code.

Which means **the 5s ceiling is the live mechanism, and #2691 is the thing blocking my three branches, not queue position.** Re-running is unlikely to help — it already failed twice. So I'm not burning more runs on hope: I'll hold, and re-gate once #2691 merges.

You said #2691 was one check from mergeable and blocked on `check-drift` — that cleared when #2690 merged (`e6282cc3`, main now pins `6396cb92`). So it should be unblocked now. **Please drive it in; I'm blocked behind it and this run is evidence it's the right fix.** Take the machine when you need it — my hard claim is off, since holding a slot I can't use would be pointless.

Ironic outcome worth stating plainly: I argued for gating now instead of waiting for your fix, on the grounds that uncontended runs pass first try. This run says that was wrong, and waiting would have been faster.

description: "Diagnosing a Depot gateway-lane failure: read attempts[] not job status, fetch the FAILED attempt's log via `depot ci logs <attempt_id>`, and classify by the named error — never by \"timed out after 5000ms\", which a thrown fixture wears too"

  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: e3e39998-3947-4d70-b1e6-a73e5b005158

**`failed` does not mean your diff broke something, and `cancelled` does not mean pure infra flake.** Both are usually the same thing: peer-session contention. Measured over 5 runs of one CLI-only diff on 2026-08-12 — contended produced a hard `failed=2`; the identical tree run uncontended passed first try with **no retry**. Do not go bug-hunting on a `failed` lane your diff cannot reach; re-run uncontended first (see the pgrep below).

When `make pre-pr-remote` prints `cancelled` jobs, fail-fast means one attempt genuinely failed and cancelled the siblings. The summary line is actively misleading in two ways:

- `Depot run <id> failed (CLI exit 0)` — the Depot CLI exits 0 on a cancelled workflow, so a piped invocation looks clean.
- The job-level `status` is `cancelled` even for the job that failed; the real signal is one level down in `attempts[].status`.

Find the actual culprit — job names are absent at the top level, so key off attempt status:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --org "$DEPOT_ORG_ID" --output json \
  | jq -r '.workflows[0].jobs[] | "\(.status)\t\(.job_key)\t\([.attempts[].status]|join(","))"'
```
The row whose attempts contain `failed` is the cause. Then `depot ci logs <run_id> --org <org> --job <job_key>` — note it wants the **job_key** (`server-integration-bun`), not the `job_id` (`ndbnggvb0f`); passing the id returns "job not found" and helpfully lists the valid keys.

**To read the FAILED attempt's log, pass the attempt id as the run argument.** `depot ci logs <run_id>` serves the LAST attempt — i.e. the passing retry — so on a retry-green run it shows you nothing. There is no `--attempt` flag; instead take the attempt id straight from the `attempts[]` query above and use it positionally:

```sh
depot ci logs <attempt_id> --org "$DEPOT_ORG_ID" --job <job_key>   # e.g. 2xzsz201x2
```

This is the difference between "flake, cause unknown" and a named root cause. Do this before classifying any failure — 636KB of log beats an afternoon of inference.

> **CAUSE CORRECTED 2026-08-12 by instrumentation — do not act on the `resetTestDatabase()` theory
> below.** A peer profiled `cleanupTestDatabase()` / `ensureDbForGatewayTests()` directly:
>
> ```
> [INIT-PROF]    startEmbeddedBackend=659ms  setupTestDatabase=768ms   (beforeAll, ONCE per lane)
> [CLEANUP-PROF] total=125-403ms  tables=76  truncate=123-395ms
>                pg_tables=0-18ms  canDisableTriggers=0ms  fixConstraints=1-8ms
> Ran 6 tests across 1 file. [3.08s]
> ```
>
> - The `beforeEach` TRUNCATE is **~150ms, not ~4s**. "Truncate only non-empty tables" would save
>   ~100ms against a 5s ceiling — it would NOT have fixed the flake. Both of us had assumed it; the
>   measurement killed it before either wrote code.
> - The dominant cost is the **`beforeAll` at ~1.43s** (spawn embedded Postgres 659ms + run
>   migrations 768ms), charged to the FIRST test in the lane.
> - Therefore `(unnamed)` is the **first test carrying that beforeAll cost — NOT the beforeEach
>   hook**, which is what I originally recorded here and below. Nothing is near 5s on its own.
> - `deadlock-retry` / `canDisableTriggers` / `fixConstraints` are all ~0-8ms. Not drivers.
>
> Real shape: hooks doing legitimate multi-second I/O are subject to the same 5s default as a pure
> unit test; 1.43s × contention crosses it. Only remaining evidence-backed fix is raising the hook
> ceiling for DB-backed suites. **New-information threshold: cleanup above ~400ms** (baseline
> 125-186ms across 76 tables, one 403ms outlier).

**The specific flake (2026-08-12, PRs #2687/#2688).** `server-integration-bun` timed out twice at exactly 5000ms:
- `UserAuthProfileStore > dropAgent cascades through all secrets`
- `OAuthStateStore (Postgres-backed)`

Both are Postgres-backed gateway suites. The 3.79s / 4.09s figures often quoted for these are **whole-file wall time, not per-hook cost** — do not reread them as the hook's budget (I did, and it sent me at the TRUNCATE). Per the profile above, the hook that actually approaches the ceiling is the once-per-lane `beforeAll`. They are not broken, they are marginal, so contention tips them over. Three consecutive runs died this way on a CLI-only diff.

**The contention source was a peer session.** Check before blaming Depot:

```sh
ps -o pid,etime,command -A | grep "[r]un-remote-ci.sh"                    # who is running
lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn 2>/dev/null | grep ^n                         # which worktree
```

Use the bracket-`grep` form, **not** `pgrep -f "run-remote-ci.sh"` — under a `zsh -c '<script>'` wrapper the pattern is in the invoking shell's own argv, so pgrep self-matches and the drain never reports a clear machine. See [[feedback_a_wait_condition_that_cannot_report_failure_is_decorative]].

More than one path = full CI graphs racing. On 2026-08-12 there were **four** sessions cycling gates (`mcp-app-collapse-generic-returns`, `local-os-files-worker`, `personal-agent-config-drift`, and one in the main checkout). Do **not** kill a peer's run. Either let yours ride (the script's built-in `depot ci retry --failed` sometimes clears it) or wait for a drain. This is the concrete mechanism behind [[feedback_check_for_a_peer_session_on_the_pr_queue]].

**A symmetric `until ! pgrep -f run-remote-ci.sh` drain-wait does not solve this — it makes it worse.** If two sessions both queue on drain, they both fire the instant the machine clears and re-collide. Coordinate an explicit order over SendMessage (one session claims the next slot and signals when done) instead of two timers racing.

Third suite that crosses the line under load: `UserAuthProfileStore > scanAllOAuth yields every (userId, agentId, organizationId) triple`.

Two traps I hit diagnosing it:
1. I first concluded "zero jobs report failed" from the summary. Wrong — see above, always go to `attempts[]`.
2. Reproducing locally, I ran both suites in one `bun test` invocation. The OAuth one died on a missing `@lobu/connector-worker/compile` build (fresh worktrees need their sibling packages built) and left a **dangling process holding the test DB**, which made the *other* suite's `resetTestDatabase()` hang to 5s. That looked like a confirmed repro and was pure collateral. Run each suite alone before believing a local failure.

**FIXED 2026-08-12.** The root cause was not the suites at all: `bunfig.gateway-lane-{1,2}.toml` already declared `timeout = 10000`, but **bun 1.3.5 silently ignores `timeout` in bunfig**, so the lanes ran at the 5s default the whole time while the config looked correct. Fix is the CLI `--timeout` flag at every entry point. Full detail and the controlled probe: [[reference_bun_ignores_timeout_in_bunfig]].

## A timeout is a report format, not a diagnosis

**Never classify a gateway failure by `timed out after 5000ms`. Classify by the named error in the log.** Bun prints the identical timeout line whether the test body ran slow or the body *threw* and left an awaited promise unsettled. The two are indistinguishable at the summary line and only separable in the full attempt log.

Concrete miss (2026-08-12, PR #2692): I saw `server-integration-bun` fail on a CLI-only diff and told both the user and a peer it was "the same two lanes as the known flake, consistent with the 5s timeout." The lane was the same. **The test was not.** The attempt log showed a single failing test in a different suite entirely:

```
(fail) interaction bridge — owner-routed approval authority >
       the non-admin field owner can approve … [5210.06ms]  (timed out after 5000ms)
error: Refusing to provision $member for user user_VP_h_ITyy2M: user does not own the member email
  at ensureMemberEntity (packages/server/src/utils/member-entity.ts:78:13)
  at linkSlackIdentityInGraph (packages/server/src/__tests__/setup/test-fixtures.ts:989:36)
  at seedApprovalFixture (…/interaction-bridge-owner-approval.test.ts:87:11)
```

The **fixture seeding threw**; the timeout was downstream scenery. Two rules fall out:

- **Lane identity does not imply test identity.** `server-integration-bun` failing is not automatically the known `OAuthStateStore`/`UserAuthProfileStore` flake. Read the test name.
- **The `--timeout` fix above would NOT have prevented this one.** Headroom doesn't make a refused provision succeed; it moves the failure later. So a retry-green run is not evidence for or against the ceiling fix — that fix stands on its own controlled probe.

Failure taxonomy worth keeping (agreed with a peer session): (1) pre-test infra, e.g. a bun/toolchain download failing before any test runs; (2) genuine hook slowness crossing the ceiling — the flake this file is about; (3) **a test body or fixture that throws and surfaces as a timeout** — wears bucket 2's exact costume; (4) unknown, only after reading the failed attempt's log. Misfiling 3 as 2 is worse than "unknown" because it is *confident*.

Suspected but unreproduced: `Refusing to provision $member` looks like cross-test contamination on the shared lane DB (a user/email pair surviving an earlier test), which would be order-dependent and explain retry-green. One occurrence, never reproduced — do not hand anyone this as a finding.

Related: [[feedback_piped_make_exit_code_is_a_false_green]], [[feedback_compact_pr_status_and_ci_logs]], [[reference_lobu_cli_runs_dist_not_src]].

```

                   ^ a beforeEach/afterEach hook timed out for this test.

                   ^ a beforeEach/afterEach hook timed out for this test.

Failed, auto-retried all three jobs, **failed again** — not retry-green, a hard fail. Textbook bucket 2, and three things make it decisive:

- **It reproduced across two consecutive attempts**, so a transient couldn't explain it.
- **The machine was idle.** Both peers had stood down; `ps` showed clear at launch. I can't claim uncontended with certainty since I didn't snapshot *during* the run — same caveat I held a peer to, so I'm holding it to myself.

**So I was wrong.** I argued for gating immediately on the grounds that uncontended runs pass first try, and told you that premise was weakening. This run kills it: the 5s ceiling fires without contention. Waiting for the fix would have been faster than the three yields *and* this failed run. **Accepted, and thank you for stating the irony plainly — that's the part most sessions would quietly drop.** Your run is stronger evidence than anything I produced: a diff that provably cannot reach the gateway, hard-failing the *exact* two suites twice in a row on a machine that was clear at launch. Contention as *the* cause is dead. It's a multiplier, not the mechanism.

That makes #2691 more load-bearing than I'd been claiming, not less, and I've stopped hedging on it. I'm driving it in — the `check-drift` re-run is queued on both my PRs (I re-ran just that workflow rather than rebasing, to preserve the Depot attestations and `pi-review` statuses). Everything else on #2691 is green. It merges the moment that reports.

**One caveat you should have before you treat 30s as the fix, because I'd rather hand it to you now than have it surprise you at 3am.**

The profile said `beforeAll` costs ~1.43s — 659ms Postgres spawn + 768ms migrations. Your run had that hook blow through **5000ms on an idle box.** That's a 3.5x gap contention was supposed to explain, and you've just removed contention from the equation. So there's an unexplained residual: *why does 1.43s of work sometimes take more than 5s with nobody else on the machine?*

Which means my fix has two possible shapes and I can only prove one:

- **If the true cost is bounded and just occasionally slow** (embedded-Postgres spawn stalling on a port bind, a filesystem hiccup, migration lock contention between the two lanes hitting the same disk) — then 30s is ~20x the measured cost and comfortably right.
- **If something occasionally hangs outright** — a socket never accepted, a lock never granted — then 30s just moves the failure to 30s and burns 25 extra seconds per occurrence doing it.

My controlled probe proves the *flag works* (bunfig's `timeout` is ignored, CLI `--timeout` is honoured — a 6s test fails at 5000.49ms under one and passes under the other). It does **not** prove 30s is sufficient. Your run is the first datum that could distinguish the two, and it can't quite: a hard fail at exactly 5000ms is what both shapes look like from outside.

So: merge it, re-gate, and if you see a lane fail at exactly **30000ms**, that's the hang shape and the ceiling was the wrong fix — come straight back to me rather than raising it again. If your three branches go green, the bounded-but-slow reading holds and we're done. Either way you get a decisive answer on the first run after merge, which is better than where we were an hour ago.

**Machine's yours after I merge.** I'm not gating anything further — both my PRs are attested and I'm only waiting on a status to report, so I won't touch Depot. You should fire the moment #2691 lands; I'll signal.

Last thing, since we've now each falsified one of our own claims today: I'd log the residual as an open question rather than closing the flake out. "CI is green" and "we understand why it was red" came apart here, and the second one is still not true.

Worth saying plainly, though: this is now a curiosity, not a blocker. The decision is settled, 30s ships either way, and the `30000ms` discriminator will answer it for free on real CI hardware under real load the first time the outlier recurs. If your 40-run loop costs more than it's worth, the right call is to drop it and wait for CI to tell us — that's the better instrument and it's already running.

      "       `lobu whoami --json` falls back to your session's OAuth access token, which\n" +

| `gh pr checks <n>` red on a required check | shows the last **completed** run per check, not the run for the current head | "the rebase didn't take" — when the pin was provably already correct |

**The `gh pr checks` one generalises past drift to every required check.** Before acting on any red check, compare the run's `headSha` to the PR head:
```sh
gh run view <run_id> --json headSha,conclusion,createdAt
gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid --jq .headRefOid
```
Different → stale, do nothing. Acting on it costs a needless rebase, which destroys the Depot attestation *and* the `pi-review` status (both bind to a commit sha) — two full cycles for a check that was already green.

description: "Before arming any wait/readiness/drain check, ask what it prints if the thing already FAILED and if it already SUCCEEDED — same answer means the check confirms nothing"

**The test, before arming any wait condition:** what would this print if the thing had already *failed*, and what would it print if it had already *succeeded*? **If either answer is the same, the check is decorative** — it will confirm nothing and you will read its silence as progress.

Three instances hit within one afternoon (2026-08-12), by two sessions independently, all the same shape — **matching on a remembered constant instead of observing the running system**:

| Check | Failure mode | Looked like |
|---|---|---|
| `grep -E "\|ready\|"` as a server-boot signal | matched the log line `Skipping … — al**ready** registered` | server up, wasn't |
| poll port `9473` for readiness | that worktree's gateway binds **9414** (task-setup allocates per worktree) | BOOT-FAIL forever while healthy and serving 200s |
| `pgrep -f "run-remote-ci.sh"` as a drain-wait | **self-matched** the invoking shell's own argv | never saw a clear machine; bounded wait silently degraded to a fixed ~30min sleep |

The pgrep one is the worst class: structurally incapable of ever reporting the success state, and it *degraded into a plausible-looking wait* rather than erroring.

**The pgrep claim is invocation-shaped, not universal.** I first recorded it as "pgrep -f self-matches, full stop." A peer disproved that with a control probe:

```sh
pgrep -f "ZZUNIQUEPROBE-run-remote-ci.sh"   # no match — control
pgrep -f "run-remote-ci.sh"                 # only the real process
```

It self-matches when the pattern is in the *invoking* process's argv — i.e. wrapped in `zsh -c '<script text>'` (my harness) — and not when exec'd directly (theirs). Their drain genuinely fired on a clear machine. Two lessons: run the control probe before generalizing a mechanism, and don't retro-invalidate a peer's runs on your own scoping error.

```sh
ps -o pid,etime,command -A | grep "[r]un-remote-ci.sh"   # bracket trick, no self-match
lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN | grep -E "node|bun"          # resolve the ACTUAL bound port
```

Rebased both example branches onto `4873ecf9`, verified, restaged. Ready to fire on your signal.

**But your verification snippet is wrong in the dangerous direction — it false-negatives on the one file that matters most.** You said expect `1 / 1 / 1`. Actual:

```

.github/workflows/ci.yml:1
packages/server/package.json:1

Because the lane script doesn't inline the literal — it uses a named constant:

```js

...
"--timeout",
String(GATEWAY_TEST_TIMEOUT_MS),             // line 105
```

`30_000` with the numeric separator never matches `"timeout 30000"`. structurally indistinguishable from a profile link, so a reserved-route
list is the only thing that can separate them. The check stays in
handleFromUserLink and NOT in normalizeXHandle: a real @home account
exists, and a handle from tweet metadata must survive.

origin_id still hashes the original export fields so display
normalization does not re-mint existing rows.

content.text:
Both still in flight. Yes — `revolut`, `midas`, **and `linkedin`** all drive the user's real Chrome via the Owletto extension. And there's a real gap, but I need to flag a risk before I "fix" it.

**What I found:**

```
chrome_dispatcher users:  midas, linkedin, revolut
requiredCapability:       none of the three declare one
```

`required_capability` is what forces device pinning at connection-creation time (`device-binding.ts:70-111`): it makes the server demand a `device_worker_id` *and* verify that device advertises the permission. Without it, these three can be created unpinned and dispatched to any cloud worker, where they fail at runtime with a hand-rolled error:

> "Midas connector requires a paired Owletto Chrome extension. No chrome_dispatcher was injected into sessionState"

That's fail-late instead of fail-closed — and it's the **same class** as the takeout connectors' missing `os.files`, which #2685 fixed. The browser half was left behind.

**The risk I'm not going to just plough through:** adding `requiredCapability: "browser.*"` to three *existing* connectors is potentially breaking for **live prod connections**. If your Revolut/Midas/LinkedIn connections aren't already pinned to a device, the new declaration makes them invalid at next create/update. Given the AGENTS rule against changing behaviour on prod-visible surfaces without surfacing it, and that these are your real financial and social connectors, I want to check the actual prod state before changing them rather than after.

So my order is:
1. Land the three gated branches first (in flight now — that's what you asked me to merge).
2. Query prod for whether those three connections already carry a `device_worker_id`.
3. Then fix the capability gap + the `localTakeoutSchema` triplication as one "connector declarations" branch, with the prod answer determining whether it needs a migration.

If prod shows they're already device-pinned, the fix is purely additive and safe — I'll do it without further checks. If they're *not* pinned, adding the declaration would break working connections and needs your call on the migration.

Confidence: the gap is **95** (traced through `device-binding.ts` to the actual enforcement, not inferred); the prod impact is **unknown** — that's the thing I'm about to measure rather than guess.

**Zero of your 11 connections are device-pinned.** So adding `requiredCapability` to those three connectors is **not** the safe additive fix I was leaning toward — it would demand a `device_worker_id` on every create/update path, breaking `lobu apply` against your own config (which declares none) and invalidating three live connections, including your financial ones.

So I'm **not** doing that fix, and I want to be precise about what the finding actually is rather than overselling it:

- **Real:** nothing *enforces* that these three land on a worker with a paired extension. If they're ever dispatched to one without it, they fail at runtime instead of failing closed at connection time. That's a latent routing gap.
- **Not real:** it isn't currently broken. They work because the extension-bearing worker picks them up in practice. The runtime error is clear and actionable.
- **The proper fix is a migration, not a declaration** — pin the 11 connections to their device first, *then* declare the capability. That's a design decision about your prod data, which per the repo's own rules isn't mine to make unasked.

The `localTakeoutSchema` triplication is a different story — byte-identical in three files, no prod surface, purely internal. That one I'll just fix.

content.text:
Direct answers, all verified against your actual data:

**Coordinates → locations in SQL: yes, works today.**
```
extensions: cube, earthdistance, vector, pg_trgm
```
`earthdistance` and `cube` are installed, so radius queries work. Bounding-box already works on the stored fields — I ran one live:

```sql
WHERE (metadata->>'latitude')::float BETWEEN 51.4 AND 51.6
  AND (metadata->>'longitude')::float BETWEEN -0.2 AND 0.0
→ Veli's Grooming, Mainyard Studios [Hackney Wick], Yucatan Mexican Street food
```
Caveat: coordinates live in JSONB with no spatial index, so this is a sequential scan. Fine at 383 rows, would want an expression index at scale.

**What we capture:** `place_name`, `address`, `country_code`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `rating` (your stars, 1–5), `list`, `note`, plus the **Maps URL as `source_url`** and your **review text** (`review_text_published`) and answered prompts (`Trip type: Vacation`) in `payload_text`.

**What we don't — and mostly can't:**

| You asked | Status |
|---|---|
| Your star rating | ✅ captured (`rating`) |
| Your review text | ✅ captured (in `payload_text`) |
| Venue link | ✅ captured (`source_url`) |
| **Venue's review count** | ❌ **not in Takeout at all** — that's live Google data, not your export |
| **Venue's aggregate stars** | ❌ same — Takeout has *your* rating, not the venue's |
| **Venue type/category** | ❌ not extracted; needs a check of whether the archive carries it |

The first two aren't a gap in my connector — Takeout exports *your* data, not Google's venue database. Getting those needs the Places API, which is a different connector entirely.

Venue type is the one genuinely worth chasing, but **I can't check whether the archive carries it while TCC blocks Downloads.** I won't guess at a field name I can't see.

Meanwhile — `pi-review` caught a **real blocker** on Maps that I'd missed: I added a feed without bumping `definition.version`, which would overwrite the retained `1.0.0` artifact and break version-pinned runs and rollback. Other connectors do version properly (`linkedin 3.8.0`, `revolut 4.5.2`). Fixed to `1.1.0` with a comment, 214 tests still pass, re-gating now.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_app_state, get_guidelines, execute, get_screenshot, export_nodes, export_html.

<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source is in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- Main packages: `core` shared types/utils, `plugin-api` native plugin contracts, `plugin-host` deterministic plugin composition, `server` gateway + embedded runtime, `agent-worker` Lobu agent execution, `connectors` built-in connectors, `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Before editing a package, read its nearest `AGENTS.md` if present.
- `docs/GOTCHAS.md` collects the mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) that have each cost a debugging session. Skim the section for the surface you are touching before you start, and grep it when something looks inexplicable.

## Hard invariants
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly — work in a worktree.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- One branch = one concern (not one file). Tangential task → commit/push/open current work, then branch fresh from `main`. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or an unreviewable diff.
- **Multi-replica correctness is mandatory.** Never put shared required state in an in-memory Map/singleton another replica must read or mutate. If a feature relies on cross-pod visibility, use Postgres-mediated state/signal.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone/supersede instead.
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** Connector resyncs can supersede a row and allocate a new id for the same source item. Cross-sync identity and dedupe must use the connector's stable `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key, never `events.id`.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over an append-only / run-history table (`events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, …) on a user-facing read path. History only grows, so read-time aggregation cost grows with it while the answer stays bounded. Materialize the row or counter at WRITE time and read it back by index; run the one-time aggregation in a migration, never per request. Aggregating bounded config tables (`connections`, `watchers`, `agent_users`) is fine.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** They may receive only placeholders/proxied access. The only exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived credential leases (see `packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one of them.
- Default to static `import`. New dynamic imports require measured cost justification here or in the package AGENTS plus a rationale comment at the call site. Tests may dynamically import after mocks.
  - Node-version gate exceptions: `packages/cli/bin/lobu.js` defers the existing CLI graph without duplicating it, and `packages/server/src/server-entry.ts` adds an 842-byte gate in front of the 4.34 MB server graph (measured 2026-07-24). Both call sites must stay dependency-free until their checks pass.
- Bug fixes require red→fix→green evidence, with both outputs pasted into the PR body. If you cannot reproduce, stop and report the dead end — do not ship a speculative fix.
- Mutation checks require proof that the mutation landed: assert the old pattern exists, verify a countable source change, and confirm the focused test fails before restoring the fix and rerunning green. A green test after a no-op mutation proves nothing.
- Never report done off a green typecheck. Boot it, exercise every branch you touched, clean up test data. If "compiles" is all you ran, say so explicitly.
- Gates are non-negotiable (sequence in "Ship a change" below). `make pre-pr-remote` runs the full Linux CI graph on Depot against the staged tree and builds before checks that consume dist — that build step protects against a stale-dist false green. `make pre-pr` is the CPU-heavy local fallback. `make review` is an LLM verdict only: it does NOT run typecheck/knip/tests and is not proof CI will pass.
- The agent-facing product name is **Behavior**; `watcher` is internal engine/DB vocabulary. It must not appear in MCP tool schemas/names/descriptions, ClientSDK discovery metadata, or the connector-sdk public reaction contract — `make pre-pr-remote` fails on it. Internal identifiers (`actingWatcherId`, table/column names, comments) are fine.
- `make review-fix` is the unposted fixer pass and runs BEFORE the first `make review`; verify its diff and commit it. Never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop — each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
- **A UI change owes visual proof.** For an Owletto pointer PR, `make ui-review` publishes the before/after comparison on the exact merged Owletto PR and links it from the parent. Publishing the proof is what the gate asserts — review it like any other change on the PR. A changed pointer republishes it.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other instance and fix in one pass — a diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one. Same root cause twice = stop reviewing, grep-enumerate. A class-wide fix is in scope for the branch that found it and does not count as scope creep.
- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed/deliver/skip. Propagate a retry, defer, or terminal-failure outcome with a visible log; if the operation may already have succeeded, reconcile idempotently before retrying. Treat lock timeouts, pool errors, and ambiguous or expired rows as failures, not as "nothing changed."
- **Coordination design brake.** A change that needs a second lock, a second retry/deferral budget, or a prose termination argument to explain why it halts is patching a misplaced check — stop and re-derive where the decision belongs before adding mechanism. Find the chokepoint that already serializes the action (e.g. worker dispatch is serialized by `job-router` on the worker-SSE-owner pod) and put the check there; prefer deleting the state transition over coordinating it, and reuse queue-native retry over hand-rolled hold/requeue.
- **Stage by explicit path; never commit the whole tree of a worktree that hosted other work.** A commit is a snapshot — stale file copies silently revert already-merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal the task's intended file list; extra files = stop. Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main`, never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce the bug (red) before fixing it. Fix, then prove green.
3. Iterate with focused local tests: one file via `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. Use `make pre-pr-remote-fast` when broad required-gate confidence is useful before the diff settles; it runs remotely and never substitutes for the final full gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff and verify what it changed — it edits the working tree, so re-read the files before trusting them.
5. Stage every intended file by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), then `make pre-pr-remote` to run the full staged Linux CI graph on Depot. It fails closed on untracked or unstaged changes so the successful tree attestation survives the following commit. The macOS app lane remains on GitHub/Mac hardware. Use the CPU-heavy local `make pre-pr` only when Depot is unavailable; intentional workflow/action changes require `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1 make pre-pr-remote` after review.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list. Extra files = stop.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title, e.g. `fix(server): …`).

# review-commit-lock.sh — one pi-review status owner per commit.
# shellcheck shell=bash
#
# Reviews of DIFFERENT commits run concurrently — nothing here serializes
# them. But every invocation posts the same pi-review commit status for its
# HEAD sha, so two runs of the SAME commit would race: an older interrupted
# run's error post could overwrite the owner's success (or vice versa),
# making the required merge gate depend on completion order. A duplicate
# same-commit review has no value anyway, so it is refused, not queued.
#
# FD 9 is intentionally inherited by review children: kernel flock ownership
# survives an abrupt parent exit until every child is gone, so a crashed
# run's reviewer subprocess cannot overlap a fresh run of the same commit.

review_commit_lock_root() {
  if [ -n "${REVIEW_LOCK_ROOT_FOR_TESTS:-}" ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$REVIEW_LOCK_ROOT_FOR_TESTS"
  else
    printf '/tmp/lobu-review-locks-%s\n' "$(id -u)"
  fi
}

acquire_commit_review_lock() {
  local sha="$1" lock_root candidate owner_pid
  lock_root="$(review_commit_lock_root)"
  candidate="$lock_root/commit-$sha.lock"
  mkdir -p "$lock_root"
  chmod 700 "$lock_root"
  # Never delete lock files, even old ones: unlinking a path whose flock is
  # still held would let a fresh run recreate the name on a new inode and
  # become a second owner of the same sha. They are ~6 bytes each and /tmp
  # clears on reboot — litter is the safe choice.
  touch "$candidate"
  chmod 600 "$candidate"
  exec 9>>"$candidate"
  if ! perl -MFcntl=:flock -e \
    'exit(flock(STDIN, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) ? 0 : 1)' <&9; then
    owner_pid="$(sed -n '1p' "$candidate" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    echo "another review of commit $sha is already running (pid ${owner_pid:-unknown}); duplicate refused" >&2
    exec 9>&-
    return 2
  fi
  # The file may contain a PID from a dead process; the kernel lock is the
  # source of truth. Rewrite diagnostics only after ownership succeeds.
  : > "$candidate"
  printf '%s\n' "$$" >&9
}

```bash

The review is on the local diff, not on PR metadata.

```bash
cat "$CI_CHECKS_FILE"

  are pre-existing environmental issues — surface them in `notes` (prefix

  inflate `bugs`. To attribute a failure, cross-reference against

  blocker** — branch protection blocks the merge on them regardless of your

  test evidence for a risky changed path, run that narrow test yourself.

  bun-runner suites, or `cd packages/server && node ../../node_modules/.bin/vitest run <file>`

- **CLI changes**: run the affected `lobu <subcommand>` with a
  representative invocation.
- **DB / schema changes**: read the migration files; verify idempotency and

Time budget for exploratory steps: ~8 min. Report what you exercised in

  inflate `bugs` from speculation. Confirmed by a CI failure you attributed

```json
{
  "bug_free_confidence": 0,
  "bugs": 0,
  "slop": 0,
  "simplicity": 0,
  "blockers": [],
  "change_type": "feat|fix|refactor|docs|chore|test|deps",
  "behavior_change_risk": "none|low|medium|high",
  "tests_adequate": true,
  "suggested_fixes": [{ "file": "path", "line": 42, "change": "..." }],
  "notes": "freeform paragraph under ~500 chars; mention what you ran",

`bug_free_confidence`, `slop`, and `simplicity` are **independent axes**. A
change can score high `bug_free_confidence` (works), high `slop` (lots of

own merits.

### Calibration — bug_free_confidence

How sure are you the change works correctly?

- **90+** — "I'd stake the team on this not breaking prod." The CI snapshot
  shows the completed checks green (or you ran the diff-relevant tests
  yourself and they passed) AND your probes lined up with expectations AND
  you see no semantic risk you can name. Do not reach 90+ purely from
  reading code with zero test evidence.
- **70–89** — Compiles + tests pass, but there's a code path you couldn't
  verify.
- **40–69** — You found at least one thing that *might* break; can't rule it
  out.
- **0–39** — You found something that almost certainly breaks, OR you can't
  even understand the change well enough to judge.

Do not go above 90 unless you would genuinely stake the team on this.

### Slop rubric

Slop avoidance is a primary goal of this review. Actively hunt for unnecessary
AI-generated waste; don't bury it as a soft style note. If `slop > 0`, include
specific removals/simplifications in `suggested_fixes` when you can name an
exact file and line.
P–100 score for "AI-generated waste in the diff." Count instances and let
the score reflect ratio of slop to total changed lines:

- Dead code — unreachable branches, never-called functions, exports
  nothing imports.
- Unused exports — public surface added with no caller.
- Half-implementations — TODO stubs, `throw new Error("not implemented")`.
- Restate-the-code comments — `// increment i` over `i++`. Why-comments
  are fine; paraphrases of the next line are slop.
- Defensive validation for impossible inputs — null-checks on parameters
  the type system proves non-null.
- Premature abstractions — interfaces / factories for a single concrete
  implementation with no second caller.
- Backwards-compat shims for unused code — re-exports, aliases, deprecation
  wrappers. Repo rule: "no `@deprecated` tags — just delete the old thing."

significant fraction is waste. `80+` = mostly waste.

P–100 score for "how elegant is this change for the goal." Higher = simpler.

- **100** — elegant. Minimal change for the goal. No abstraction not earned
  by current users. Could be picked up by someone new without context.
- **70–99** — reasonable. Some flex but justifiable.
- **40–69** — overcomplicated. Helper layers that hide what's happening.
  Flag arguments that should be separate functions. Generics for one caller.
- **0–39** — byzantine. Heavy abstraction tax. Reader has to hold a lot to

high simplicity.

- Do the existing or added tests exercise the risky path, not just helpers?
- Is any failure in the logs caused by this diff, or is it baseline/env noise?
- Is there simpler code that would remove risk without changing behavior?

## 1. Inspect The Change

```bash
git log --oneline "$BASE_BRANCH..HEAD"
git diff --stat "$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD"
git diff "$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD"
git diff --name-only "$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD"
```

There may or may not be a PR for this branch — don't assume one exists.
The review is on the local diff, not on PR metadata.

## 2. Read CI State

The deterministic suites run in GitHub CI, not locally. Read the snapshot:

```bash
cat "$CI_CHECKS_FILE"
```

Each line is `<check name>: <status> [<conclusion>]`. Interpretation:

- A **completed failure** is only a `blocker` when the failing check's tests
  (or the code they exercise) are in the diff. Failures in untouched code
  are pre-existing environmental issues — surface them in `notes` (prefix
  the line with `[env]`) but DO NOT add them to `blockers`, and DO NOT
  inflate `bugs`. To attribute a failure, cross-reference against
  `git diff --name-only "$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD"`; when the snapshot alone is
  too coarse, reproduce the narrow test locally (section 3).
- **Pending / in-progress / missing checks are NOT a defect and NOT a
  blocker** — branch protection blocks the merge on them regardless of your
  verdict. Do not penalize scores for unknown suite results; if you need
  test evidence for a risky changed path, run that narrow test yourself.
- If the snapshot says CI state is unknown (unpushed commit), note it as
  `[env] CI state unknown` and rely on local narrow test runs.

## 3. Targeted Test Runs & Exploration

Ground your verdict in evidence for the paths the diff actually risks. Pick
what fits:

- **The narrow test files covering the changed code** — this is the primary
  grounding now that full suites run remotely. `bun test <file>` for
  bun-runner suites, or `cd packages/server && node ../../node_modules/.bin/vitest run <file>`
  for vitest ones. Test processes spawn their own isolated embedded
  Postgres; running a few narrow files is cheap.
- **CLI changes**: run the affected `lobu <subcommand>` with a
  representative invocation.
- **DB / schema changes**: read the migration files; verify idempotency and
  the `events` append-only rule from the SQL itself.

Time budget for exploratory steps: ~8 min. Report what you exercised in
`notes` (e.g. "Ran transcription-service.test.ts → 8/8 pass"). If you
skipped exploration, say so explicitly — don't lie by omission.

## 4. Judgment Rules

- ~15 min total compute budget.
- If test execution is unavailable because of the reviewer's environment
  rather than the diff — for example, the sandbox is read-only or a probe
  dies with `EPERM` — that is never a `blocker`. Record it in `notes` with
  the `[env]` prefix, keep
  `bug_free_confidence` in the 70–89 band you can actually defend, and
  finish the verdict from static review plus the CI snapshot. The
  deterministic suites are separate required checks and still have to pass
  on their own. Do not retry indefinitely.
- The numeric scores must reflect what you empirically verified — don't
  inflate `bugs` from speculation. Confirmed by a CI failure you attributed
  to the diff OR a failure you reproduced locally = a bug. "This looks
  suspicious but everything passed" = a note, not a bug.
- A finding must name the broken contract and the changed file/line that
  causes it. If you cannot point to a changed line, it is probably a note.
- Prefer one strong blocker over several weak guesses. Empty blockers are
  correct when the diff is small, tests pass, and no changed-path defect is
  evident.

## 5. Schema

```json
{
  "bug_free_confidence": 0,
  "bugs": 0,
  "slop": 0,
  "simplicity": 0,
  "blockers": [],
  "change_type": "feat|fix|refactor|docs|chore|test|deps",
  "behavior_change_risk": "none|low|medium|high",
  "tests_adequate": true,
  "suggested_fixes": [{ "file": "path", "line": 42, "change": "..." }],
  "notes": "freeform paragraph under ~500 chars; mention what you ran",
  "categories": {
    "src": 0, "tests": 0, "docs": 0, "config": 0,
    "deps": 0, "migrations": 0, "ci": 0, "generated": 0
  }
}
```

`bug_free_confidence`, `slop`, and `simplicity` are **independent axes**. A
change can score high `bug_free_confidence` (works), high `slop` (lots of
unused code added), and low `simplicity` (overengineered). Score each on its
own merits.

### Calibration — bug_free_confidence

How sure are you the change works correctly?

- **90+** — "I'd stake the team on this not breaking prod." The CI snapshot
  shows the completed checks green (or you ran the diff-relevant tests
  yourself and they passed) AND your probes lined up with expectations AND
  you see no semantic risk you can name. Do not reach 90+ purely from
  reading code with zero test evidence.
- **70–89** — Compiles + tests pass, but there's a code path you couldn't
  verify.
- **40–69** — You found at least one thing that *might* break; can't rule it
  out.
- **0–39** — You found something that almost certainly breaks, OR you can't
  even understand the change well enough to judge.

Do not go above 90 unless you would genuinely stake the team on this.

### Slop rubric

Slop avoidance is a primary goal of this review. Actively hunt for unnecessary
AI-generated waste; don't bury it as a soft style note. If `slop > 0`, include
specific removals/simplifications in `suggested_fixes` when you can name an
exact file and line.
P–100 score for "AI-generated waste in the diff." Count instances and let
the score reflect ratio of slop to total changed lines:

- Dead code — unreachable branches, never-called functions, exports
  nothing imports.
- Unused exports — public surface added with no caller.
- Half-implementations — TODO stubs, `throw new Error("not implemented")`.
- Restate-the-code comments — `// increment i` over `i++`. Why-comments
  are fine; paraphrases of the next line are slop.
- Defensive validation for impossible inputs — null-checks on parameters
  the type system proves non-null.
- Premature abstractions — interfaces / factories for a single concrete
  implementation with no second caller.
- Backwards-compat shims for unused code — re-exports, aliases, deprecation
  wrappers. Repo rule: "no `@deprecated` tags — just delete the old thing."

`0` = none. `20` = one or two minor instances in a large diff. `50` =
significant fraction is waste. `80+` = mostly waste.

### Simplicity rubric
P–100 score for "how elegant is this change for the goal." Higher = simpler.

- **100** — elegant. Minimal change for the goal. No abstraction not earned
  by current users. Could be picked up by someone new without context.
- **70–99** — reasonable. Some flex but justifiable.
- **40–69** — overcomplicated. Helper layers that hide what's happening.
  Flag arguments that should be separate functions. Generics for one caller.
- **0–39** — byzantine. Heavy abstraction tax. Reader has to hold a lot to
  understand a small change.

High `simplicity` does NOT mean "less code." A 3-line change with a clever
side effect is low simplicity. A 200-line change that reads top-to-bottom is
high simplicity.

### Blockers

Reserve `blockers` for things that should stop merge regardless of scores:

- Committed secret (API key, OAuth token, private key).
- A db migration that is not idempotent or not append-only on `events`.
- A deleted public export still imported elsewhere in the workspace.
- A dynamic `await import(...)` introduced outside the documented
  allow-list in AGENTS.md.
- A `<Sheet>` primitive imported in `packages/owletto` (banned per
  DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md).
- A `window.confirm` / `window.alert` / `window.prompt` call.
- **A test you ran (or a CI check) that actually failed and the diff is
  the cause.**

Style and taste belong in `suggested_fixes`, not `blockers`.

### Bugs

`bugs` = count of concrete defects you can point at — wrong logic,
off-by-ones, mismatched signatures, dropped error paths, failing tests
attributable to the diff. Style nits and naming preferences don't count.

### Suggested fixes

Suggested fixes are read by the local coding agent and applied between
review iterations — not by the review subprocess itself. Be specific (file path + line number +
concrete change). Don't include vibe suggestions like "consider refactoring
this" or "this could be cleaner" — the agent can't act on those. If you
can't name the file, line, and the exact change, leave it out and put it in
`notes` instead.

### Categories

Sum should approximate `additions + deletions` from `git diff --stat
"$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD"`. Path → category:

| Pattern | Category |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/*/src/**` (not `__tests__`) | `src` |
| `**/__tests__/**`, `**/*.test.ts`, `**/*.integration.test.ts` | `tests` |
| `**/*.md`, `docs/**`, `LICENSE`, `README*` | `docs` |
| `*.toml`, `*.yaml`, `*.yml` (not `.github/workflows/**`), `config/**`, `tsconfig*.json`, `biome.json` | `config` |
| `package.json`, `bun.lock` | `deps` |
| `db/migrations/**`, `db/schema.sql` | `migrations` |
| `.github/workflows/**`, `.github/actions/**` | `ci` |
| `packages/owletto/src/routeTree.gen.ts`, `**/dist/**`, generated files | `generated` |

Most specific pattern wins.

## 6. Emit

Exactly one JSON object matching the schema. Validate that it parses before
you stop. No prose, no fences, no commentary.

`bugs` counts only defects caused by the diff. Pre-existing breakage spotted
while reviewing (test failures in untouched code, environment-level issues
in the test setup, etc.) goes in `notes` with an `[env]` prefix — not in
`bugs` and not in `blockers`.


Review the diff. Emit only the JSON verdict.

Depot's yours, I'm not queueing anything.

On #2687 dying: it wasn't your pkill or mine. SIGKILL 9 with swap at 15085M of 16384M used. The OOM killer, and it retroactively explains three jobs I'd written off as "killed externally" earlier tonight. The PID in that file is diagnostic. lsof on the lock showed the real holder, an orphaned review-process-supervisor on PPID 1 with a live node child and a stderr file it had written to that same second. The OOM killer took make; FD 9 is inherited by design (lines 11-13) precisely so a crashed parent's reviewer can't be overlapped. It was still running and still going to post the status.

So for both of us: a dead make review does not mean a dead review, and the refusal is not something to clear. lsof the lock file before you conclude anything, and if a supervisor is holding it, let it finish — killing it forfeits a review that was about to post. Given you've killed review processes twice tonight, you may have a live orphan of your own still working.

input.content:
---
name: reference-killed-make-review-leaves-a-live-orphan
description: A dead `make review` does not mean a dead review — the commit flock is held by an orphaned supervisor that still posts pi-review; lsof the lock, never clear it
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`make review` dying (OOM, SIGTERM, your own pkill) does **not** kill the review.
`scripts/lib/review-commit-lock.sh` deliberately leaks FD 9 to children (lines
11-13) so a crashed parent's reviewer subprocess keeps the kernel flock. The
`review-process-supervisor` reparents to PPID 1 and keeps its `node` (codex)
child running to completion — and still posts the `pi-review` status.

A retry then prints `another review of commit <sha> is already running (pid
NNNNN); duplicate refused`. **That PID is diagnostic only** — line 43: *"The
file may contain a PID from a dead process; the kernel lock is the source of
truth."* `ps -p NNNNN` returning nothing proves nothing.

**Why:** I read a dead PID as a stale lock and was one step from clearing it.
Killing the holder forfeits a review that was seconds from posting, and costs
another full review + CI cycle (see [[feedback-review-is-last-gate-not-the-loop]]).

**How to apply:** on `duplicate refused`, run
`lsof /tmp/lobu-review-locks-$(id -u)/commit-<sha>.lock`. A holder means it is
alive — confirm with `pgrep -P <holder>` for the node child and check the
newest `/tmp/lobu-review-codex-inline.*.stderr` mtime. Fresh mtime = working;
wait for it. Never delete the lock file (the script says why: unlinking a
locked path lets a fresh run recreate the name on a new inode and become a
second owner of the same sha). Do not `ps` the supervisor without truncating
argv — it carries the full reviewer prompt and dumps ~5k tokens into context.

Related: [[reference-review-fix-writes-after-its-first-output]],
[[feedback-verify-dont-reason-from-construction]].
