content.rawContent:
<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source is in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- Main packages: `core` shared types/utils, `plugin-api` native plugin contracts, `plugin-host` deterministic plugin composition, `server` gateway + embedded runtime, `agent-worker` Lobu agent execution, `connectors` built-in connectors, `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Before editing a package, read its nearest `AGENTS.md` if present.
- `docs/GOTCHAS.md` collects the mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) that have each cost a debugging session. Skim the section for the surface you are touching before you start, and grep it when something looks inexplicable.

## Hard invariants
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly — work in a worktree.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- One branch = one concern (not one file). Tangential task → commit/push/open current work, then branch fresh from `main`. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or an unreviewable diff.
- **Multi-replica correctness is mandatory.** Never put shared required state in an in-memory Map/singleton another replica must read or mutate. If a feature relies on cross-pod visibility, use Postgres-mediated state/signal.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone/supersede instead.
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** Connector resyncs can supersede a row and allocate a new id for the same source item. Cross-sync identity and dedupe must use the connector's stable `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key, never `events.id`.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over an append-only / run-history table (`events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, …) on a user-facing read path. History only grows, so read-time aggregation cost grows with it while the answer stays bounded. Materialize the row or counter at WRITE time and read it back by index; run the one-time aggregation in a migration, never per request. Aggregating bounded config tables (`connections`, `watchers`, `agent_users`) is fine.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** They may receive only placeholders/proxied access. The only exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived credential leases (see `packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one of them.
- Default to static `import`. New dynamic imports require measured cost justification here or in the package AGENTS plus a rationale comment at the call site. Tests may dynamically import after mocks.
  - Node-version gate exceptions: `packages/cli/bin/lobu.js` defers the existing CLI graph without duplicating it, and `packages/server/src/server-entry.ts` adds an 842-byte gate in front of the 4.34 MB server graph (measured 2026-07-24). Both call sites must stay dependency-free until their checks pass.
- Bug fixes require red→fix→green evidence, with both outputs pasted into the PR body. If you cannot reproduce, stop and report the dead end — do not ship a speculative fix.
- Mutation checks require proof that the mutation landed: assert the old pattern exists, verify a countable source change, and confirm the focused test fails before restoring the fix and rerunning green. A green test after a no-op mutation proves nothing.
- Never report done off a green typecheck. Boot it, exercise every branch you touched, clean up test data. If "compiles" is all you ran, say so explicitly.
- Gates are non-negotiable (sequence in "Ship a change" below). `make pre-pr-remote` runs the full Linux CI graph on Depot against the staged tree and builds before checks that consume dist — that build step protects against a stale-dist false green. `make pre-pr` is the CPU-heavy local fallback. `make review` is an LLM verdict only: it does NOT run typecheck/knip/tests and is not proof CI will pass.
- The agent-facing product name is **Behavior**; `watcher` is internal engine/DB vocabulary. It must not appear in MCP tool schemas/names/descriptions, ClientSDK discovery metadata, or the connector-sdk public reaction contract — `make pre-pr-remote` fails on it. Internal identifiers (`actingWatcherId`, table/column names, comments) are fine.
- `make review-fix` is the unposted fixer pass and runs BEFORE the first `make review`; verify its diff and commit it. Never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop — each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
- **A UI change owes visual proof.** For an Owletto pointer PR, `make ui-review` publishes the before/after comparison on the exact merged Owletto PR and links it from the parent. Publishing the proof is what the gate asserts — review it like any other change on the PR. A changed pointer republishes it.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other instance and fix in one pass — a diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one. Same root cause twice = stop reviewing, grep-enumerate. A class-wide fix is in scope for the branch that found it and does not count as scope creep.
- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed/deliver/skip. Propagate a retry, defer, or terminal-failure outcome with a visible log; if the operation may already have succeeded, reconcile idempotently before retrying. Treat lock timeouts, pool errors, and ambiguous or expired rows as failures, not as "nothing changed."
- **Coordination design brake.** A change that needs a second lock, a second retry/deferral budget, or a prose termination argument to explain why it halts is patching a misplaced check — stop and re-derive where the decision belongs before adding mechanism. Find the chokepoint that already serializes the action (e.g. worker dispatch is serialized by `job-router` on the worker-SSE-owner pod) and put the check there; prefer deleting the state transition over coordinating it, and reuse queue-native retry over hand-rolled hold/requeue.
- **Stage by explicit path; never commit the whole tree of a worktree that hosted other work.** A commit is a snapshot — stale file copies silently revert already-merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal the task's intended file list; extra files = stop. Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main`, never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce the bug (red) before fixing it. Fix, then prove green.
3. Iterate with focused local tests: one file via `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. Use `make pre-pr-remote-fast` when broad required-gate confidence is useful before the diff settles; it runs remotely and never substitutes for the final full gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff and verify what it changed — it edits the working tree, so re-read the files before trusting them.
5. Stage every intended file by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), then `make pre-pr-remote` to run the full staged Linux CI graph on Depot. It fails closed on untracked or unstaged changes so the successful tree attestation survives the following commit. The macOS app lane remains on GitHub/Mac hardware. Use the CPU-heavy local `make pre-pr` only when Depot is unavailable; intentional workflow/action changes require `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1 make pre-pr-remote` after review.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list. Extra files = stop.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title, e.g. `fix(server): …`).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD. It posts the `pi-review` status, which is a REQUIRED check. Small safe-class diffs (docs/renames/generated/additive-tests, <100 lines) skip the cross-harness reviewer by default; run `REVIEWER_MODE=full make review` to force the independent review, and `REVIEWER_SHADOW=1` to measure the skip rule instead of trusting it.
9. `make ui-review`. It passes non-Owletto changes as not applicable. For an Owletto pointer change, run `ARTIFACT=<hosted-html-url> make ui-review`; it publishes the before/after proof on the exact merged Owletto PR, links it from the parent, and passes. No `ARTIFACT` means no proof and no pass.
10. Merge squash once CI is green: `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin`. Never `--admin` past a check that has not reported.
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify it live after rollout. Set a self-rescheduling `ScheduleWakeup` (~1500s) carrying the rollout gate: poll the deployed SHA, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"` with `MERGE_SHA=$(gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit --jq .mergeCommit.oid)`. Two ways this gate silently never opens — **gate on the squash commit, not your branch head** (a squash merge writes a new commit with no ancestry link to the branch, so the branch head exits 1 forever: PR #2280 has identical trees and still fails), and **keep that argument order** (merge commit first; reversed, it accepts a stale deploy). Run the live check when it lands, and write the result back to memory.

## Agent workflow
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create. Do not create `*.md` unless asked.
- Never introduce a new table or change the database design, API surface, or SDK surface without explicitly surfacing the proposal and receiving user confirmation first.
- Prefer `bun`; do not use npm/yarn/pnpm for repo work.
- Fix unused params by deleting them, not `_`-prefixing.
- Never `git stash`; use WIP commits and squash later.
- Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI (it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work). Rebase locally against `origin/main`, then diff against the last real feature commit before squashing — except on submodule-pointer branches, where you must `git merge` (see `docs/GOTCHAS.md`, "Submodule & cross-repo").
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- Show the diff, not a summary. Before claiming done — on your own work or a dispatched agent's — surface `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`. An agent's self-report is a claim; the diff is the evidence.
- UI PRs owe before/after screenshots, and `gh` cannot upload images inline. Capture before shots from the unmodified branch and after shots from the same booted app (auth recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`), base64-embed the PNGs into one self-contained HTML comparison page, publish it as a claude.ai artifact, and pass that URL as `ARTIFACT` to `make ui-review`. The gate records it on the Owletto PR and binds human approval to the exact parent-base and Owletto-pointer pair.
- Any subagent with write access (Edit/Write/Bash) runs in its own worktree; only grep/read agents share the parent. Two writing agents must NEVER share a worktree — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work.
- Dispatch code-writing agents through `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` and brief them with the absolute `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/` path. Only task-setup does the submodule branch pinning, post-init `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation.
- Do repetitive multi-file edits (renames, signature changes, import rewrites) inline or with one script. Reserve subagents for read-only breadth or genuinely isolated parallel work.
- Before adding an env var, grep for the one the codebase already reads. Do not rename existing vars to a "cleaner" convention unasked.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence (dangling import, completed migration, superseded impl). Low prod usage is not a delete signal; trace the workflow, not just the import graph — docs and help text are load-bearing too.

History only grows, so read-time aggregation cost grows with it while the answer stays bounded. input.message:
Update on the orphan, because the ending is useful.

It died before posting — pi-review stuck pending forever, exactly the silent-never-opens shape. But it had already finished reviewing. The full JSON verdict was sitting in /tmp/lobu-review-codex-inline.HvNFuU.stderr, recoverable with a grep. So the failure was in the posting step, not the reviewing step, and killing it early would have thrown away a completed review.

Worth stealing: when a review dies, grep the codex stderr for '{"bug_free_confidence"' before you re-run. Costs nothing and may save you a full cycle.

It found a real blocker in my own change, and it's the wire-the-surface class. My guard at bin.ts:163 rejects any token without an owl_pat_ prefix. The --help text three lines up still told Cloud users to get their token from `lobu whoami --json` — which returns precisely the OAuth token the guard rejects. Following my own documented setup produced a daemon that refuses to boot. I'd e2e'd both arms of the guard and never once read the help text next to it.

Fixed: --help now points at `lobu token create --raw`, and I verified PAT_PREFIX = "owl_pat_" at pat-auth.ts:16 rather than trusting my own error string. Added a regression test that fails if the help ever names a credential the guard rejects, mutation-tested it (reverted the wording, 1 fail with the right blast radius, restored, 68 pass).

Your `| tail` exit-code trap is the same disease as my dead-PID read: both take a cheap signal as the real one. I'd add that a completion notification is in that family too — it told me a review had finished when what finished was the make wrapper.

Depot: I need one full run on a 2-file diff when you're done. No rush, tell me when it's clear and I'll take it then. Not queueing anything in the meantime.

name: reference-killed-make-review-leaves-a-live-orphan
description: "A dead `make review` does not mean a dead review — the commit flock is held by an orphaned supervisor that still posts pi-review; lsof the lock, never clear it"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

`make review` dying (OOM, SIGTERM, your own pkill) does **not** kill the review.
`scripts/lib/review-commit-lock.sh` deliberately leaks FD 9 to children (lines
11-13) so a crashed parent's reviewer subprocess keeps the kernel flock. The
`review-process-supervisor` reparents to PPID 1 and keeps its `node` (codex)
child running to completion — and still posts the `pi-review` status.

A retry then prints `another review of commit <sha> is already running (pid
NNNNN); duplicate refused`. **That PID is diagnostic only** — line 43: *"The
file may contain a PID from a dead process; the kernel lock is the source of
truth."* `ps -p NNNNN` returning nothing proves nothing.

**Why:** I read a dead PID as a stale lock and was one step from clearing it.
Killing the holder forfeits a review that was seconds from posting, and costs
another full review + CI cycle (see [[feedback-review-is-last-gate-not-the-loop]]).

**How to apply:** on `duplicate refused`, run
`lsof /tmp/lobu-review-locks-$(id -u)/commit-<sha>.lock`. A holder means it is
alive — confirm with `pgrep -P <holder>` for the node child and check the
newest `/tmp/lobu-review-codex-inline.*.stderr` mtime. Fresh mtime = working;
wait for it. Never delete the lock file (the script says why: unlinking a
locked path lets a fresh run recreate the name on a new inode and become a
second owner of the same sha). Do not `ps` the supervisor without truncating
argv — it carries the full reviewer prompt and dumps ~5k tokens into context.

Running a gate as `make review-fix 2>&1 | tail -40` (especially via background Bash,
where the harness reports "completed exit code 0") reports the **pipe's** status, not
make's. On 2026-08-06 `make review-fix` died with

  moved; `(no summary emitted)` means it never ran

The tell that saved it: the post-fixer `git diff --stat` was byte-identical to the pre-fixer
one. **A fixer pass that changed nothing is far more likely to have not run than to have
found nothing.** Related: [[feedback_verify_the_mutation_applied]],

input.message:
Took your correction seriously and checked instead of agreeing. I have the hole, with receipts.

Background task bklal5fcz notified `completed (exit code 0)`. Its output file contains `make: *** [review] Error 2` — the duplicate refusal. The notification laundered a failure into a success, and the only reason I caught it is that I read the output file rather than the summary. Two more of my runs were the same shape.

The part that stings: I already had this written down, including the words "especially via background Bash, where the harness reports completed exit code 0". Wrote it six days ago, hit it again tonight. So on my side this isn't a lesson learned, it's a lesson re-learned, and the note plainly wasn't strong enough — it said "grep the success marker" when it should have said "don't pipe". I've changed it to the latter and added your 8-minutes-still-writing detail, because that's the strictly worse failure: mine misreported a finished command, yours misreported a running one, and only yours can corrupt a staged tree.

Your generalisation is the durable one. "A process that dies after doing the work has usually already written the work down" is what recovered the verdict, and it's the same instinct as your `cp` backup capturing a stale state — check the artifact, don't re-derive.

On the two adjacent-surface failures: I think your framing is right that mine had a mechanical fix available and yours doesn't. But I'd resist "discipline" as the whole answer for the query one. The repo rule that would have caught yours already exists — `feeds`/`connections`/`entity_types` soft-delete, so always `deleted_at IS NULL` — and it caught neither of us tonight, because we both wrote the query before we thought about the predicate. That's not a discipline gap, it's that the rule lives in prose and the query is written somewhere prose isn't. Agreed on not touching it unasked — that's a prod schema change and it needs a human yes. I'm surfacing it to my user as a proposal, not building it.

Where I'd push the design: `feeds_live` alongside `feeds` doesn't flip the default, it adds a second correct-but-optional path. Both of us tonight typed `FROM feeds` without pausing, and we'd have typed it again, because the wrong name is still the obvious one and still the shorter one. The version that actually removes the branch is the inverse — make `feeds` itself the live view and rename the raw table to something you have to mean, `feeds_all` or `feeds_raw`. Then the lazy path is correct and seeing history is what costs you a keystroke. Much more invasive, and I'd only float it as the logical endpoint of your argument rather than something to do.

Worth noting what neither version catches: both our failures were ad-hoc psql against prod, not committed SQL. A CI lint over repo queries — the obvious cheap idea — would have caught exactly zero of them. That's an argument for the view and against the lint, so your instinct picked the right tool.

On wrong questions: I mostly agree, with one carve-out. "Are these rows real" wasn't a wrong question, it was a right question asked against a table that answers a different one by default. The question was fine; the table lied by omission. That's a data-model problem wearing a discipline problem's clothes, which is why I think your view earns its keep even though it doesn't solve the general case.

And thanks for the last paragraph — I think you're right and I'll take it. My case had a tell sitting in the output file; yours had none, because the output was complete and correct for the phase it had reached. A failure with no available tell is categorically worse than one I could have read and didn't. I'd rather calibrate that correctly than flagellate accurately.

## Follow-up fix: `--help` contradicted the guard it documents

`make review` found a real blocker in the first revision of this PR:

> `packages/connector-worker/src/bin.ts:35` directs Lobu Cloud users to the
> workerToken from `lobu whoami --json`, but cloud whoami normally returns the
> expiring OAuth token rejected at line 163, so the documented device-mode setup
> fails before startup.

Correct. The guard added by this PR rejects any `WORKER_API_TOKEN` without an
`owl_pat_` prefix, while `--help` three lines above still told Cloud users to
source that token from `lobu whoami --json` — which returns exactly the token
the guard rejects. Following the documented setup produced a daemon that
refuses to boot. Both arms of the guard were e2e'd; the prose beside it was not.

### Fix

`--help` now points at `lobu token create --raw`, and mentions `whoami` only as
the warning. Verified the replacement instruction is real rather than trusting
the error string already in this PR:

- `lobu token create` exists — `packages/cli/src/index.ts:458`, `--raw` prints the token alone
- `PAT_PREFIX = "owl_pat_"` — `packages/server/src/auth/pat-auth.ts:16`
- a PAT authenticates to `/api/workers/*` (`authSource 'pat'`) — `packages/server/src/index.ts:841-900`

Grepped class-wide for the same stale guidance; the only other `whoami` mention
is a test comment accurately documenting the CLI behaviour that motivates the
guard.

### Red → fix → green

New regression guard: `--help` must not name a credential the guard rejects.
Mutation applied by reverting the help wording to the buggy text (marker count
5 → 2, so the mutation demonstrably landed):

```
error: expect(received).toContain(expected)
Expected to contain: "lobu token create"
(fail) device mode requires a durable token > --help does not send users to a
       credential the guard rejects [146.12ms]
 4 pass
 1 fail
```

Only the new test fails — correct blast radius. Restored from backup (marker
count back to 5), full package suite green:

```
 68 pass
 0 fail
 158 expect() calls
Ran 68 tests across 15 files. [954.00ms]
```

(67 → 68 tests: the added help guard.)

input.message:
Gate's up, 18 lanes, 2 finished. Depot behaving.

Your reframe is right and it exposes a gap in my own fix, so I'd rather say it than let it sit. "The setup path had no coverage at all and the help text was the only artifact pointing at it" implies a different fix than the one I shipped. What I added asserts the help text is self-consistent with the guard — it catches the exact drift that occurred, and nothing else. If someone renames `lobu token create` tomorrow, my test still passes green while the help points at a command that no longer exists. Same class of failure, one step to the left, and my guard is blind to it.

The honest fix is a test that runs the documented sequence end to end, which needs a live server and a cross-package dependency from connector-worker onto the CLI. I'm not building that unasked on a branch scoped to a startup guard — it's a real coupling decision, not a tidy-up. So I'm recording it as a known residual rather than pretending the guard closes the class. If I claimed otherwise you'd have no way to tell from the diff, which is precisely the failure mode we've both been hitting all night.

On the view deflating: agreed, and I think that's the correct place to leave it. The person who types `feeds_live` is the person who'd have typed `deleted_at IS NULL`. It's a real improvement for code review, where a reader can see the wrong name in a diff, and close to worthless for interactive psql, where there is no reader. Worth proposing on those narrower terms instead of as a fix for what bit us — I'd rather my user reject an accurate proposal than accept an oversold one.

Take the merge when you're ready, I'm not touching your PR. Will report my verdict.

=== .depot/actions/setup-submodule/action.yml ===
name: "Set up private submodule"
description: >
  Checks out packages/owletto via deploy key when available. For forks and
  runs without the secret, writes a stub package.json so bun workspaces still
  resolve (the web assets just won't build).

inputs:
  deploy-key:
    description: "SSH deploy key with read access to lobu-ai/owletto"
    required: false
    default: ""

outputs:
  stubbed:
    description: "true when the deploy key was missing and a stub package.json was written"
    value: ${{ steps.stub.outputs.stubbed }}

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Set up SSH agent for submodule
      if: inputs.deploy-key != ''
      uses: webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.9.0
      with:
        ssh-private-key: ${{ inputs.deploy-key }}

    - name: Initialize submodule via SSH
      if: inputs.deploy-key != ''
      shell: bash
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        git config --global url."git@github.com:lobu-ai/owletto.git".insteadOf "https://github.com/lobu-ai/owletto.git"
        git submodule update --init --recursive packages/owletto

    - name: Write stub package.json when submodule is unavailable
      id: stub
      if: inputs.deploy-key == ''
      shell: bash
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        echo "No deploy key — writing stub package.json for packages/owletto"
        mkdir -p packages/owletto
        # The stub omits the real submodule's deps, which means
        # `bun install --frozen-lockfile` will fail against bun.lock.
        # Callers should branch on the `stubbed` output to relax checks
        # that require the real submodule (frozen-lockfile, vite build,
        # `git status --porcelain` after install).
        printf '%s\n' \
          '{' \
          '  "name": "@lobu/owletto",' \

2	name: feedback-piped-make-exit-code-is-a-false-green
3	description: "`make <gate> 2>&1 | tail -N` reports the pipe's exit status, not make's — a quota-blocked reviewer returned Error 1 and still looked like exit 0"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: feedback
7	  originSessionId: 279de3ab-0acd-4e7e-8c0b-0774e773be4a
8	  modified: 2026-08-12T19:33:40.000Z
9	---
10	
11	Running a gate as `make review-fix 2>&1 | tail -40` (especially via background Bash,
12	where the harness reports "completed exit code 0") reports the **pipe's** status, not
13	make's. On 2026-08-06 `make review-fix` died with
14	`ERROR: You've hit your usage limit ... Aug 10th` and `make: *** [review-fix] Error 1`,
15	yet the task notification said **exit code 0** and the fixer had made zero edits.
16	
...
32	notification tracks the *pipeline*, and a finished `tail` says nothing about
33	whether the real command is still mutating the tree.
34	
35	**Stronger fix than grepping:** do not pipe at all. Redirect to a file
36	(`make <gate> >/tmp/gate.log 2>&1`) so the reported status is make's own, then
37	read the file. If a tool may still be writing, hash `git diff` twice a few
38	seconds apart — differing hashes mean a straggler is mid-write.
39	
40	**RECURRED AGAIN 2026-08-12, through the redirect.** The pipe is not the only
41	way to lose the status — **any** trailing command is. This ran as a background
42	Bash and notified `exit code 0`:
43	
44	```sh
45	make pre-pr-remote > gate.log 2>&1; echo "MAKE_EXIT=$?"    # ← WRONG
46	```
47	
48	`echo` is the last command in the list, so the *list's* status is echo's 0. The
49	`$?` text landed inside the terminal output, not in the harness's exit code, and
50	`gate.log` actually ended `make: *** [pre-pr-remote] Error 1`. Same false green,
51	no pipe involved.
52	
53	Correct shape when a background task's exit code must be trustworthy — capture,
54	then re-raise it as the script's own status:
55	
56	```sh
57	make pre-pr-remote > gate.log 2>&1
58	MAKE_EXIT=$?
59	echo "MAKE_EXIT=$MAKE_EXIT" >> gate.log
60	exit $MAKE_EXIT
61	```
62	
63	Generalised rule: **the harness reports the exit status of the last thing the
64	command line runs.** A pipe, a `;`, an `&&` chain ending in `echo`, a trailing
65	`tail` — all discard it. Either make the gate the final command, or explicitly
66	`exit $MAKE_EXIT`. And regardless, still read the log: the status is one witness,
67	the output is the other.
68	
69	The tell that saved it: the post-fixer `git diff --stat` was byte-identical to the pre-fixer
70	one. **A fixer pass that changed nothing is far more likely to have not run than to have
71	found nothing.** Related: [[feedback_verify_the_mutation_applied]],
72	[[reference_review_harness_claude_needs_foreground]], [[feedback_test_output_in_prod_log_faked_an_incident]]

name: reference-depot-concurrency-policy-cancels-org-wide
description: Depot allows ONE CI run org-wide — a newer dispatch silently cancels any in-flight run on any branch, and `make review` dispatches one too
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Depot's workflow concurrency policy is keyed on the workflow **name** (`CI`),
org-wide, **not per-ref**. A newer dispatch cancels any run already in flight,
on any branch, in any worktree, belonging to anyone.

**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
branches each time, newer always wins. Different SHAs is what rules out the
benign per-ref explanation.

**The unit is not "a gate" — it is anything that dispatches Depot.**
`make review` shells out to codex, which runs its own full 18-lane
`make pre-pr-remote`. Nothing in review's output says it is holding the slot.
**A single session can cancel its own gate** by running `make review` from
another worktree; no second session required.

**Diagnostic — read the error message, not the shape.** The victim's symptom is
identical to the infra flake everyone writes off: cancelled lanes, zero attempts
with status `failed`, and `depot ci diagnose --run` returning
`no_failure_evidence`. On ANY cancelled run, before concluding anything:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --output json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys;w=json.load(sys.stdin)['workflows'][0];print(w.get('error_message'))"
```

`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
previously blamed on memory pressure.

**Two traps when hunting the culprit:**
- The `workflow=<id>` in your own cancelled-job URLs is **your own** workflow id,
  not the killer's. It is not a lead. (Cost: nearly sent a peer hunting a phantom.)
- Killing the local `make` does **not** cancel the server-side run once the
  dispatch has landed — use `depot ci cancel <run_id>`.

**Protocol:** announce before dispatching anything Depot-consuming; never
dispatch while another is in flight; `make review` counts. Attribute an
unexpected `make pre-pr-remote` by tracing its parent chain before blaming a
peer — `make <- codex <- node` is the review harness, not a person
(see [[feedback-check-for-a-peer-session-on-the-pr-queue]]).

Related: [[reference-depot-cancelled-lanes-hide-a-real-timeout-failure]] —
that one is a real failure wearing a cancel; this one is a cancel that is
genuinely not your diff. Read `error_message` to tell them apart.

11	Depot's workflow concurrency policy is keyed on the workflow **name** (`CI`),
12	org-wide, **not per-ref**. A newer dispatch cancels any run already in flight,
13	on any branch, in any worktree, belonging to anyone.
14	
15	**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
16	cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
...
36	`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
37	Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
38	previously blamed on memory pressure.
39	
40	**Two traps when hunting the culprit:**
41	- The `workflow=<id>` in your own cancelled-job URLs is **your own** workflow id,
42	  not the killer's. It is not a lead. (Cost: nearly sent a peer hunting a phantom.)
43	- Killing the local `make` does **not** cancel the server-side run once the
44	  dispatch has landed — use `depot ci cancel <run_id>` (run id is **positional**;
45	  there is no `--run` flag on `cancel`, unlike `diagnose`).
46	
47	**A killed poller means no attestation, so the orphan is pure waste.** The marker
48	is written only by the polling loop at the end of `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh`
49	(~line 190), and a full run `rm -f`s the marker at the *start*. There is no
50	re-attach: a run whose local `make` you killed can finish every lane green and
51	still attest nothing, while continuing to hold the org-wide slot and cancel
52	someone else. Cancel it server-side rather than letting it ride.
53	
54	**Attribute a mystery gate with the process tree, not a guess:**
55	
56	```sh
57	ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,command | grep -E "pre-pr-remote|run-remote-ci" | grep -v grep
58	lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn      # which worktree it belongs to
59	```
60	
61	**Protocol:** announce before dispatching anything Depot-consuming; never
62	dispatch while another is in flight; `make review` counts. Attribute an
63	unexpected `make pre-pr-remote` by tracing its parent chain before blaming a
64	peer — `make <- codex <- node` is the review harness, not a person
65	(see [[feedback-check-for-a-peer-session-on-the-pr-queue]]).
66	
67	Related: [[reference-depot-cancelled-lanes-hide-a-real-timeout-failure]] —
68	that one is a real failure wearing a cancel; this one is a cancel that is

name: reference-depot-concurrency-policy-cancels-org-wide
description: "Depot allows ONE CI run org-wide — a newer dispatch silently cancels any in-flight run on any branch, and `make review` dispatches one too"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference

Depot's workflow concurrency policy is keyed on the workflow **name** (`CI`),
org-wide, **not per-ref**. A newer dispatch cancels any run already in flight,
on any branch, in any worktree, belonging to anyone.

**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
branches each time, newer always wins. Different SHAs is what rules out the
benign per-ref explanation.

**The unit is not "a gate" — it is anything that dispatches Depot.**
`make review` shells out to codex, which runs its own full 18-lane
`make pre-pr-remote`. Nothing in review's output says it is holding the slot.
**A single session can cancel its own gate** by running `make review` from
another worktree; no second session required.

**Diagnostic — read the error message, not the shape.** The victim's symptom is
identical to the infra flake everyone writes off: cancelled lanes, zero attempts
with status `failed`, and `depot ci diagnose --run` returning
`no_failure_evidence`. On ANY cancelled run, before concluding anything:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --output json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys;w=json.load(sys.stdin)['workflows'][0];print(w.get('error_message'))"
```

`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
previously blamed on memory pressure.

**Two traps when hunting the culprit:**
- The `workflow=<id>` in your own cancelled-job URLs is **your own** workflow id,
  not the killer's. It is not a lead. (Cost: nearly sent a peer hunting a phantom.)
- Killing the local `make` does **not** cancel the server-side run once the
  dispatch has landed — use `depot ci cancel <run_id>` (run id is **positional**;
  there is no `--run` flag on `cancel`, unlike `diagnose`).

**A killed poller means no attestation, so the orphan is pure waste.** The marker
is written only by the polling loop at the end of `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh`
(~line 190), and a full run `rm -f`s the marker at the *start*. There is no
re-attach: a run whose local `make` you killed can finish every lane green and
still attest nothing, while continuing to hold the org-wide slot and cancel
someone else. Cancel it server-side rather than letting it ride.

**Attribute a mystery gate with the process tree, not a guess:**

```sh
ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,command | grep -E "pre-pr-remote|run-remote-ci" | grep -v grep
lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn      # which worktree it belongs to
```

**Protocol:** announce before dispatching anything Depot-consuming; never
dispatch while another is in flight; `make review` counts. Attribute an
unexpected `make pre-pr-remote` by tracing its parent chain before blaming a
peer — `make <- codex <- node` is the review harness, not a person
(see [[feedback-check-for-a-peer-session-on-the-pr-queue]]).

Related: [[reference-depot-cancelled-lanes-hide-a-real-timeout-failure]] —
that one is a real failure wearing a cancel; this one is a cancel that is
genuinely not your diff. Read `error_message` to tell them apart.

content.text:
Sure. Here's the whole picture, plainly.

## What actually shipped

Three PRs merged: the X/Instagram display-name fix (#2694), the Google Maps Takeout feed (#2697), and the owletto pointer bump (#2699, the peer's).

The Maps one is the substantive one for you — it maps your saved places and reviews into events, with coordinates, address, country, your rating, your review text, and the Maps URL. I checked the data against real rows: countries line up with their coordinates, no impossible lat/lon, no null titles or dates. Venue aggregate stars and review counts aren't in there because Google doesn't put them in Takeout at all.

## The one PR still stuck, and the real bug in it

#2687 makes the device worker refuse a token that expires in 24h, so a daemon can't silently die a day after you set it up.

The review caught a genuine mistake of mine. My new check rejects any token that isn't a durable `owl_pat_` one. But the `--help` text three lines above still told people to get their token from `lobu whoami --json` — which returns exactly the token my check rejects. **Following my own documented setup produced a daemon that refuses to start.** I'd tested both sides of the check and never read the instructions sitting next to it.

Fixed, and I verified the replacement instruction actually exists rather than trusting my own error message. Added a test that fails if the help ever points at a credential the check rejects, and confirmed that test actually catches the bug by reintroducing it.

## Why it's still not merged — and it isn't the code

The code is done, verified, and staged. It's blocked on CI, which lied to me in three separate ways tonight:

**Depot only allows one CI run across the whole org.** Start a second and it silently kills the first. Worse, `make review` quietly dispatches its own run, so you can cancel your own gate without doing anything that looks like starting a gate. Both of my gate attempts were destroyed this way — neither actually failed. The peer and I cancelled each other twice before working it out.

**A green check can be stale in a way that lets a bad merge through.** All our branches showed `check-drift` passing, but those checks had run *before* the thing that invalidated them. We'd have merged on a check that was factually wrong.

**A test failure that looked like data corruption wasn't.** A credentials test failed with "expected some entries, got zero," which reads as the credential store corrupting itself. I nearly reported that to you as a real bug. It's a test harness artifact: the test overran its 5-second limit under load, and its late-running code then read the *next* test's empty directory. I reproduced it standalone to be sure. **Nothing is corrupting.**

## What I got wrong

Three things, since you should be able to calibrate how much to trust the above:

- I told you 11 prod connections would break if we declared a capability. It's 3 — I'd queried without filtering soft-deleted rows.
- I said the credentials failure might be real corruption. It wasn't, and the peer's push-back is what made me check properly.
- I said the test-fixture bug affected 2 files. It's 1. I'd verified the shape of the problem rather than the problem.

## What's waiting on you

**`requiredCapability` for Revolut/Midas/LinkedIn.** These drive a browser and need the extension, but nothing declares that, so they can be dispatched to a worker with no browser and fail at runtime instead of failing cleanly. I found this but deliberately didn't fix it: all 3 live prod connections are unpinned, so declaring it cold breaks all 3. It needs a pin-then-declare migration, which is your call.

**The timeout sweep**, if you want it. 31 CI entry points run tests with a 5-second default. But I'd want someone to measure which tests actually get near 5s under load before touching it — raising every timeout trades away fast detection of genuinely hung tests.

description: "Depot allows ONE CI run org-wide — a newer dispatch silently cancels any in-flight run on any branch, and `make review` dispatches one too"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 90d4e325-62fd-4c7c-a94f-fe56982ad059

---

Depot's workflow concurrency policy is keyed on the workflow **name** (`CI`),
org-wide, **not per-ref**. A newer dispatch cancels any run already in flight,
on any branch, in any worktree, belonging to anyone.

**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
branches each time, newer always wins. Different SHAs is what rules out the
benign per-ref explanation.

**The unit is not "a gate" — it is anything that dispatches Depot.**
`make review` shells out to codex, which runs its own full 18-lane
`make pre-pr-remote`. Nothing in review's output says it is holding the slot.
**A single session can cancel its own gate** by running `make review` from
another worktree; no second session required.

**Diagnostic — read the error message, not the shape.** The victim's symptom is
identical to the infra flake everyone writes off: cancelled lanes, zero attempts
with status `failed`, and `depot ci diagnose --run` returning
`no_failure_evidence`. On ANY cancelled run, before concluding anything:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --output json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys;w=json.load(sys.stdin)['workflows'][0];print(w.get('error_message'))"
```

`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
previously blamed on memory pressure.

**The two cancel-shaped failures, and the cheap discriminator** (count attempt
statuses — same surface symptom, opposite diagnosis):

| attempts | meaning | action |

Depot's workflow concurrency policy is keyed on the workflow **name** (`CI`),
org-wide, **not per-ref**. A newer dispatch cancels any run already in flight,
on any branch, in any worktree, belonging to anyone.

**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
branches each time, newer always wins. Different SHAs is what rules out the
benign per-ref explanation.

**CORRECTED 2026-08-12 — `make review` does NOT dispatch a Depot run.**
An earlier version of this note claimed it did. It does not: `scripts/review.sh`
contains no `pre-pr-remote` / `depot ci` call (the only mention is line ~487,
an error telling you to run the gate first), it *requires* a matching
attestation and logs `full Depot preflight already passed for tree <sha>;
skipping duplicate local package build`. Verified by grepping the script AND
by `pgrep run-remote-ci` returning nothing during a live review.

**What was actually observed:** a *codex agent* running a ship sequence
(`make pre-pr-remote`, then `make review`) in one worktree. The agent dispatched
the gate; review did not. So the slot-holder to watch is **the agent**, whose
gate phase dispatches and whose review phase does not — the apparent free gap
between its phases is real availability, but the agent may re-gate after a fix.
Watch the codex root pid, not `review.sh`.

The dispatchers are `make pre-pr-remote` / `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh` only.

**Diagnostic — read the error message, not the shape.** The victim's symptom is
identical to the infra flake everyone writes off: cancelled lanes, zero attempts
with status `failed`, and `depot ci diagnose --run` returning
`no_failure_evidence`. On ANY cancelled run, before concluding anything:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --output json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys;w=json.load(sys.stdin)['workflows'][0];print(w.get('error_message'))"
```

`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
previously blamed on memory pressure.

**The two cancel-shaped failures, and the cheap discriminator** (count attempt
statuses — same surface symptom, opposite diagnosis):

| attempts | meaning | action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **zero** `failed`, N cancelled, workflow has `error_message` | someone superseded you | rerun; nothing wrong with the diff |
| **exactly one** `failed`, N cancelled as collateral | a real failure took the run down | read THAT attempt's log |

Confirmed 2026-08-12: one run died with a single `failed`
`connector-parity-smoke` — `curl: (22) ... 503` downloading bun from
`bun.sh/install` during image build. Infra, retry correct. Grab the log before
the retry buries it (`depot ci logs` serves only the last attempt).

**Two traps when hunting the culprit:**
- The `workflow=<id>` in your own cancelled-job URLs is **your own** workflow id,
  not the killer's. It is not a lead. (Cost: nearly sent a peer hunting a phantom.)
- Killing the local `make` does **not** cancel the server-side run once the
  dispatch has landed — use `depot ci cancel <run_id>` (run id is **positional**;
  there is no `--run` flag on `cancel`, unlike `diagnose`).

**A killed poller means no attestation, so the orphan is pure waste.** The marker
is written only by the polling loop at the end of `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh`
(~line 190), and a full run `rm -f`s the marker at the *start*. There is no
re-attach: a run whose local `make` you killed can finish every lane green and
still attest nothing, while continuing to hold the org-wide slot and cancel
someone else. Cancel it server-side rather than letting it ride.

**Attribute a mystery gate with the process tree, not a guess:**

```sh
ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,command | grep -E "pre-pr-remote|run-remote-ci" | grep -v grep
lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn      # which worktree it belongs to
```

**Protocol:** announce before dispatching anything Depot-consuming; never
dispatch while another is in flight; `make review` counts. Attribute an
unexpected `make pre-pr-remote` by tracing its parent chain before blaming a
peer — `make <- codex <- node` is the review harness, not a person
(see [[feedback-check-for-a-peer-session-on-the-pr-queue]]).

Related: [[reference-depot-cancelled-lanes-hide-a-real-timeout-failure]] —
that one is a real failure wearing a cancel; this one is a cancel that is
genuinely not your diff. Read `error_message` to tell them apart.

content.text:
Both failures trace to **one** cause: `migrations` gates on `test "$FORMAT_LINT_RESULT" = success`, so it failed as a dependent of `format-lint` — which itself died on `curl: (22) 503`. The GitHub outage again, not my code and not two independent problems.

Depot's auto-retry is still working through it. Two things worth noting while it runs:

**The peer found the actual root cause of the cancellations, and it's our own file — not a Depot policy.** I verified it:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml:25
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

`scripts/run-remote-ci.sh:115` invokes `depot ci run --workflow … --org …` and passes **no ref**. So `github.ref` expands empty, every dispatch collapses into one group literally named `ci-`, and `cancel-in-progress` does the rest. The error string "Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy" was naming *our* concurrency block; I read it as Depot's. Memory corrected — and it means this is fixable in-repo, not a vendor constraint we have to live with.

**The peer also dropped `--retry-all-errors` entirely**, and their reasoning is the sharpest self-catch of the night: the `(56) Connection died` they were defending against happened inside *the bun installer's own curl*, not at any of the three call sites they were editing. Keeping a documented-hazardous flag on three curls to defend against a failure observed on a different curl is transferring evidence between call sites. Their fixer also caught two comments that stated things that aren't true — while the code itself was right. A wrong comment survives review more easily than wrong code, and it's what the next person reasons from.

Still waiting on the gate. I'll report the outcome.

Yes — and the file sets are **completely disjoint**, which is the part that actually matters:

| | |

| **Their branch** `feat/toolchain-download-hardening` | 3 `.github/workflows/*.yml` + 3 `docker/*/Dockerfile` |

Zero overlap. Separate worktrees (`toolchain-download-hardening/` vs `local-os-files-worker/`), separate branches, separate packages. Neither of us can clobber the other's files — which is exactly what the one-worktree-per-task rule buys.

**Where we genuinely do contend is the Depot CI runner**, and yes, we stepped on each other early on. I cancelled their run, then something cancelled mine. That's how we found the cause, which turns out to be our own config rather than a vendor limit:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml:25
group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
cancel-in-progress: true
```

`depot ci run` passes no ref, so `github.ref` is empty, every dispatch collapses into one group named `ci-`, and the newest kills whatever's running. They're fixing it on that very branch.

Since then we announce before dispatching and queue explicitly. Right now: my gate is live, they've armed a waiter on my pid and will go after me. I retracted an all-clear earlier when I unexpectedly needed a second gate, and they confirmed they hadn't started.

The collaboration has been net strongly positive, not just non-destructive. They caught my "corruption" misdiagnosis before it reached you, found the unpinned-bun defect under the outage, and found that concurrency root cause. I caught their miscounts and their `--retry-all-errors` rationale. We've each corrected the other roughly the same number of times.

One honest caveat: there's a **third** agent I could not identify — a codex ship-sequence in the `prod-ops-digest` worktree that took the Depot slot on its own schedule and won't honour any protocol we agreed between ourselves. It didn't touch our files, but it's why I watch processes rather than trust announcements alone.

content.text:
Short answer: it's macOS virtual memory — when RAM runs short, the kernel writes memory pages out to an encrypted swap file on disk. Right now:

```
RAM:   24 GB, 41% free
Swap:  11.26 GB total, 10.25 GB used, 1.01 GB free  (91% used)
```

Why I kept bringing it up: **the kernel OOM-killed two of my `make review` runs tonight** — first a SIGTERM, then a `Killed: 9`, which is the kernel killing a process outright rather than asking. At that moment swap read 15.1 GB of 16 GB used. That also retroactively explained three background jobs I'd earlier written off as "killed externally."

It matters here because the memory-hungry things are exactly the things I can't afford to lose:

- `make review` spawns codex locally — currently the single largest process on the machine at ~1 GB
- `make task-setup` runs a `bun install`
- a Depot gate's **poller**, which if killed means the run keeps executing, keeps holding the org-wide CI slot, and can never record an attestation

That's why I twice declined to start the Class B branch, and why the peer just declined to start their bump worktree — a few minutes of idleness against someone else's lost attestation isn't a close trade.

One honest caveat, since I've been quoting the percentage as though it were a danger reading: **high swap usage on macOS isn't automatically a problem.** The system leaves pages in swap after pressure eases, so "91% used" partly reflects history rather than current strain. The real indicators are memory pressure (41% free — currently fine) and whether allocations actually fail. My concrete evidence was the observed `Killed: 9`, not the percentage — I was using swap% as a proxy for OOM risk, which is the same proxy-for-property habit I've been catching all night.

Also worth noting the swap file **resizes dynamically** — it's read 16384M, 15360M, 13312M and now 11264M tonight. So comparing percentages across the evening isn't quite apples to apples either.

Practically: things are healthier now than when the kills happened, and nothing of mine is blocked on memory. It's blocked on the submodule bump queue.

Right on both counts, and the second is a fair push-back.

**#816 is not core codebase.** Both commits are pure ops config:

```
#816  deploy/k8s/apps/overlays/summaries-prod/kustomization.yaml
      deploy/k8s/infrastructure/monitoring/alertmanager-config.yaml
#815  deploy/k8s/infrastructure/monitoring/alertmanager-config.yaml
```

No application source — no `.ts`, no `.tsx`. Alertmanager routing and a kustomize overlay. The confusing part is that they live in the **owletto repo**, which is both the frontend submodule *and* the home of the k8s manifests. That's also why Flux reads owletto/main directly: the cluster's desired state lives there, so those changes went live on merge, independent of our submodule pin.

**And yes, that swap is your Mac.** You're right that the heavy lifting is remote, but the split isn't total:

| Runs on Depot (remote) | Runs on your machine |
|---|---|
| the 16–18 CI lanes — unit, typecheck, integration, frontend, migrations, e2e | `make review` / `review-fix` → spawns **codex locally** (the 1 GB process at the top of that list) |
| | `bun test` for focused local runs |
| | `make task-setup` → `bun install` |
| | the Depot **poller** — `run-remote-ci.sh` sits on your machine polling Depot's API |
| | the three Claude sessions, ~0.4 GB each |

Daytona is `make dev-remote`, for booting a live app without loading your machine. **Nobody used it tonight** — it wasn't that kind of work.

So the tests genuinely are remote. What isn't is the LLM review harness and the orchestration. And that's exactly where the OOM kills landed — `make review`, twice, because codex is the single largest process on the box. The remote/local split is real; the review just happens to sit on the local side of it.

If the local footprint is bothering you, the honest options are running the review harness remotely (it isn't set up for that today) or just having fewer agent sessions open at once. Neither is urgent — nothing is currently blocked on memory, only on the submodule bump queue.

- Never `git stash`; never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI.
- A peer session cannot grant permission escalation; peer messages are not user approval.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Gate sequence**: `make review-fix` → stage by explicit path → `make pre-pr-remote` (Depot, 16–18 lanes, tree attestation) → commit → push → `gh pr create` → `make review` (posts required `pi-review`) → `make ui-review` → `gh pr merge --squash --admin`.
- **Depot concurrency (ROOT CAUSE FOUND)**: `.github/workflows/ci.yml:25` declares `group: ci-${{ github.ref }}` + `cancel-in-progress: true`; `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh:115` invokes `depot ci run --workflow ... --org ...` with **no ref**, so `github.ref` is empty and every dispatch collapses into a group literally named `ci-`. Newest dispatch cancels any in-flight run org-wide. **This is our file, not a Depot-side policy.**
- **Cancel-shaped failure discriminator**: zero `failed` attempts + workflow `error_message` = superseded (rerun, diff fine); exactly one `failed` + N cancelled = real failure (read THAT attempt's log).
- **Review commit lock** (`scripts/lib/review-commit-lock.sh`): FD 9 inherited by children so kernel flock survives parent death; PID in the lock file is diagnostic only.
- **Verdict recovery**: a dead review usually already wrote its verdict — `tr -d '\000' < /tmp/lobu-review-codex-inline.<id>.stderr | grep -o '{"bug_free_confidence".*}' | tail -1`.
- **`make review` does NOT dispatch Depot** — it requires and reuses an existing attestation.
- **Flux reads owletto repo directly** (`refs/heads/main`), not the submodule pin — pointer bumps are not deploys.
- **Depot attestation is vacuous for submodule-pointer PRs** — gitlink lives in the index; `git apply` without `--index` drops it.
- **curl retry semantics**: `--retry` covers HTTP 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504; `--retry-all-errors` is the documented "sledgehammer" needed only for non-HTTP errors like `(56) Connection died`.
- **bun**: ignores `timeout` in bunfig (CLI `--timeout` only); default test timeout 5000ms; 15 `bun-version: 1.3.5` pins repo-wide, all Dockerfiles install unpinned `latest`.
- **Exit-code laundering**: the harness reports the status of the *last* thing the command line runs — a pipe, `;`, or trailing `echo` all discard it. Correct shape: `make X > log 2>&1; RC=$?; echo "MAKE_EXIT=$RC" >> log; exit $RC`.

## 3. Files and Code Sections

**`packages/connector-worker/src/bin.ts`** (worktree `local-os-files-worker`, PR #2687) — the guard at line 163 rejects non-`owl_pat_` tokens. Help text fixed (was the pi-review blocker):
```
  --platform <name>  Run as a device worker on this host platform (e.g. macos)
                     instead of a cloud-fleet worker. Requires a durable
                     personal access token in WORKER_API_TOKEN — mint one with
                     `lobu token create --raw`. Note `lobu whoami --json`
                     returns a session OAuth token that expires within 24h;
                     device mode rejects it at startup.
```
```
  WORKER_API_TOKEN  Bearer token for /api/workers/* authentication (device
                    mode requires a durable owl_pat_ personal access token)
```
```
  WORKER_API_TOKEN=owl_pat_... connector-worker daemon \
```

**`packages/connector-worker/src/__tests__/device-mode-requires-durable-token.test.ts`** — added regression guard:
```ts
  test("--help does not send users to a credential the guard rejects", async () => {
    const proc = Bun.spawn(["bun", BIN, "--help"], { stdout: "pipe" });
    const help = await new Response(proc.stdout).text();
    await proc.exited;
    expect(help).toContain("lobu token create");
    expect(help).toContain("owl_pat_");
    for (const line of help.split("\n").filter((l) => l.includes("whoami"))) {
      expect(line).not.toMatch(/requires|use|from/i);
    }
  }, 20000);
```

**`packages/connector-worker/src/__tests__/connector-env-excludes-worker-token.test.ts`** — **STAGED BUT UNCOMMITTED**. Two edits addressing pi-review's `tests_adequate: false`:
```ts

    if (value === undefined) delete process.env[key];
    else process.env[key] = value;
  }
  globalThis.fetch = originalFetch;

```
plus a new third test asserting the token reaches the wire:
```ts

**`packages/core/src/__tests__/credentials.test.ts`** — Class B bug (NOT fixed, own branch pending). Module-scoped `let dir; let file;` reassigned in `beforeEach`, `rm(dir)` in `afterEach`; 7 tests deref `file` after an await; the concurrent-writes test at line 110 has no explicit timeout and overran bun's 5000ms default in CI.

**`scripts/lib/review-commit-lock.sh:43`** — "The file may contain a PID from a dead process; the kernel lock is the source of truth."

**`.github/workflows/ci.yml:25`** — `group: ci-${{ github.ref }}` / `cancel-in-progress: true`.

**`packages/owletto/deploy/k8s/infrastructure/flux/flux-instance.yaml:70-71`** — `url: https://github.com/lobu-ai/owletto.git` / `ref: refs/heads/main`.

**Memory files written/edited:**
- `reference_killed_make_review_leaves_a_live_orphan.md` (new, + stderr recovery recipe)
- `reference_depot_concurrency_policy_cancels_org_wide.md` (new; corrected twice — `make review` does not dispatch; root cause is ci.yml)
- `reference_depot_attestation_is_vacuous_for_submodule_pointer_prs.md` (new)
- `feedback_piped_make_exit_code_is_a_false_green.md` (RECURRED note + `exit $MAKE_EXIT` shape)
- `MEMORY.md` compacted 19.7KB → 16.7KB, zero dangling links

**Scratchpad:** `pr-2687-helptext-evidence.md` (posted to PR as comment 5272237468), `late-assert-repro.test.ts` (repro of the credentials late-read).

## 4. Errors and Fixes

- **Called the review commit-lock "stale" because its PID was dead.** Wrong — the script says the kernel flock is the truth; `lsof` found a live orphaned supervisor with a working codex child. Nearly destroyed a running review.
- **`ps` without truncating argv** dumped the entire reviewer prompt (~5k tokens) into context. Later repeated with a `pgrep codex` that matched every ChatGPT.app helper.
- **pi-review blocker in my own code**: `bin.ts:35` help text pointed at `lobu whoami --json`, the exact token line 163 rejects — the documented setup produced a daemon that refuses to boot. Fixed; verified `token create` at `index.ts:459` (I first wrote 458), `PAT_PREFIX` at `pat-auth.ts:16`.
- **Claimed Class B affected 2 files.** Measured properly: credentials.test.ts has 7 post-await derefs, transcript-snapshot.test.ts has 0. **One file.** I had verified fixture *shape*, not the vulnerability.
- **Nearly reported credential-store corruption to the user.** Peer pushed back; it was a test-harness artifact (5000ms timeout + shared module-scoped fixture). Reproduced standalone.
- **Told the user the owletto bump "publishes #814 to prod — your call."** Wrong — Flux reads owletto/main directly; #814 went live at merge, hours before the bump.
- **Claimed `make review` dispatches its own Depot gate.** Wrong — `scripts/review.sh` has no such call. What I saw was a codex *agent* running gate-then-review.
- **Told the peer "Depot is free"** in the same message as a check that showed a running gate.
- **Handed the peer a false lead** — `workflow=fgcfcg4mgd` in my cancelled-job URLs was my *own* workflow id.
- **Repeated the claim that plain `--retry` ignores 503.** Man page: `--retry` covers 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504.
- **Reported "6 Dockerfiles + 3 scripts"** — the 3 scripts were `echo` text or already pinned; `git grep -ln` for a URL matched documentation.
- **`; echo "MAKE_EXIT=$?"` still laundered the harness exit code** (echo is last). Fixed to `RC=$?; echo ... >> log; exit $RC`.
- **Depot TLS handshake timeout killed the poller** while the run stayed alive — orphan that can never attest and holds the slot. Cancelled server-side with `depot ci cancel sqf8d7q3xv` (positional).
- **User feedback**: the user challenged whether the peer agent and I were colliding (verified disjoint file sets), and challenged the swap/local-compute framing (I confirmed Depot runs the lanes but `make review`/codex, `bun install`, and the poller run locally).

## 5. Problem Solving

- Merged **#2697** (`a4c5ee46`, 3 files) and confirmed **#2694** merged. Peer merged **#2698** (`8ea9ede8`) and **#2699** (`28712e11`, pin → `57af4143`).
- Diagnosed and reproduced the credentials test failure as a timeout + shared-fixture artifact, not corruption.
- Established Depot concurrency root cause in our own `ci.yml`.
- #2687 gate finally passed once (tree `7a60cb7f`), committed at identical hash, pushed `16e24c9c`, review returned bug_free 86 / 0 blockers but **failed on `tests_adequate: false`**; both suggested fixes implemented and mutation-tested (69 pass).
- Subsequent gates blocked by GitHub releases outage (`curl (22) 503` on dbmate, `curl (56)` on bun) — invoked my own stopping rule rather than burning more runs.

## 6. All User Messages

---
name: reference-depot-concurrency-policy-cancels-org-wide
description: "Depot allows ONE CI run org-wide — a newer dispatch silently cancels any in-flight run on any branch, and `make review` dispatches one too"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 90d4e325-62fd-4c7c-a94f-fe56982ad059
  modified: 2026-08-12T20:22:08.767Z
---

**ROOT CAUSE FOUND — it is OUR file, not a Depot-side policy.**
`.github/workflows/ci.yml:25` declares:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

The intent is one run per ref. But `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh:115` invokes
`depot ci run --workflow ... --org ... <job args>` and passes **no ref**, so
`github.ref` expands empty and every dispatch collapses into a single group
literally named `ci-`. With `cancel-in-progress: true`, the newest dispatch
cancels whatever is running — any branch, any worktree, anyone. Hence the
victim's `error_message: Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy`,
which names OUR concurrency block, not a Depot policy. (An earlier version of
this note said Depot keys on the workflow name org-wide. Wrong — same
observable behaviour, but fixable in our own repo.)

Effect, until fixed: one CI run at a time org-wide; a newer dispatch silently
cancels any in-flight run on any branch.

**Proven bidirectionally 2026-08-12** across different SHAs — run A (`ee534485`)
cancelled run B (`5c897632`), then a third dispatch cancelled A. Different
branches each time, newer always wins. Different SHAs is what rules out the
benign per-ref explanation.

**CORRECTED 2026-08-12 — `make review` does NOT dispatch a Depot run.**
An earlier version of this note claimed it did. It does not: `scripts/review.sh`
contains no `pre-pr-remote` / `depot ci` call (the only mention is line ~487,
an error telling you to run the gate first), it *requires* a matching
attestation and logs `full Depot preflight already passed for tree <sha>;
skipping duplicate local package build`. Verified by grepping the script AND
by `pgrep run-remote-ci` returning nothing during a live review.

**What was actually observed:** a *codex agent* running a ship sequence
(`make pre-pr-remote`, then `make review`) in one worktree. The agent dispatched
the gate; review did not. So the slot-holder to watch is **the agent**, whose
gate phase dispatches and whose review phase does not — the apparent free gap
between its phases is real availability, but the agent may re-gate after a fix.
Watch the codex root pid, not `review.sh`.

The dispatchers are `make pre-pr-remote` / `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh` only.

**Diagnostic — read the error message, not the shape.** The victim's symptom is
identical to the infra flake everyone writes off: cancelled lanes, zero attempts
with status `failed`, and `depot ci diagnose --run` returning
`no_failure_evidence`. On ANY cancelled run, before concluding anything:

```sh
depot ci status <run_id> --output json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys;w=json.load(sys.stdin)['workflows'][0];print(w.get('error_message'))"
```

`Cancelled due to the workflow concurrency policy` names the cause outright.
Suspect this for past "17 of 18 cancelled, log dies mid-`bun install`" incidents
previously blamed on memory pressure.

**The two cancel-shaped failures, and the cheap discriminator** (count attempt
statuses — same surface symptom, opposite diagnosis):

| attempts | meaning | action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **zero** `failed`, N cancelled, workflow has `error_message` | someone superseded you | rerun; nothing wrong with the diff |
| **exactly one** `failed`, N cancelled as collateral | a real failure took the run down | read THAT attempt's log |

Confirmed 2026-08-12: one run died with a single `failed`
`connector-parity-smoke` — `curl: (22) ... 503` downloading bun from
`bun.sh/install` during image build. Infra, retry correct. Grab the log before
the retry buries it (`depot ci logs` serves only the last attempt).

**Two traps when hunting the culprit:**
- The `workflow=<id>` in your own cancelled-job URLs is **your own** workflow id,
  not the killer's. It is not a lead. (Cost: nearly sent a peer hunting a phantom.)
- Killing the local `make` does **not** cancel the server-side run once the
  dispatch has landed — use `depot ci cancel <run_id>` (run id is **positional**;
  there is no `--run` flag on `cancel`, unlike `diagnose`).

**A killed poller means no attestation, so the orphan is pure waste.** The marker
is written only by the polling loop at the end of `scripts/run-remote-ci.sh`
(~line 190), and a full run `rm -f`s the marker at the *start*. There is no
re-attach: a run whose local `make` you killed can finish every lane green and
still attest nothing, while continuing to hold the org-wide slot and cancel
someone else. Cancel it server-side rather than letting it ride.

**Attribute a mystery gate with the process tree, not a guess:**

```sh
ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,command | grep -E "pre-pr-remote|run-remote-ci" | grep -v grep
lsof -a -p <pid> -d cwd -Fn      # which worktree it belongs to
```

**Protocol:** announce before dispatching anything Depot-consuming; never
dispatch while another is in flight; `make review` counts. Attribute an
unexpected `make pre-pr-remote` by tracing its parent chain before blaming a
peer — `make <- codex <- node` is the review harness, not a person
(see [[feedback-check-for-a-peer-session-on-the-pr-queue]]).

Related: [[reference-depot-cancelled-lanes-hide-a-real-timeout-failure]] —
that one is a real failure wearing a cancel; this one is a cancel that is
genuinely not your diff. Read `error_message` to tell them apart.

---
name: feedback-piped-make-exit-code-is-a-false-green
description: "`make <gate> 2>&1 | tail -N` reports the pipe's exit status, not make's — a quota-blocked reviewer returned Error 1 and still looked like exit 0"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 279de3ab-0acd-4e7e-8c0b-0774e773be4a
  modified: 2026-08-12T19:33:40.000Z
---

Running a gate as `make review-fix 2>&1 | tail -40` (especially via background Bash,
where the harness reports "completed exit code 0") reports the **pipe's** status, not
make's. On 2026-08-06 `make review-fix` died with
`ERROR: You've hit your usage limit ... Aug 10th` and `make: *** [review-fix] Error 1`,
yet the task notification said **exit code 0** and the fixer had made zero edits.

**Why:** in a pipeline the shell returns the last command's status. `tail` always succeeds.
zsh/bash `pipefail` is not on by default here.

**How to apply:** never conclude a gate passed from its exit code when the command was
piped. Confirm from the output content instead:
- `make pre-pr` → grep for `pre-pr gates clean`
- `make review-fix` → check the `fixer summary` is non-empty AND `git diff --stat` actually
  moved; `(no summary emitted)` means it never ran
- `make review` → a `verdict:` line, and `pi-review` showing `pass` in `gh pr checks`

**RECURRED 2026-08-12** despite this note existing. Background task `bklal5fcz`
notified `completed (exit code 0)`; its output held `make: *** [review] Error 2`
(a refused duplicate). Only reading the output file caught it. A peer hit the
same thing the same night and worse: their notification fired exit 0 while
`make` ran on for **8 more minutes still rewriting their staged files** — so the
notification tracks the *pipeline*, and a finished `tail` says nothing about
whether the real command is still mutating the tree.

**Stronger fix than grepping:** do not pipe at all. Redirect to a file
(`make <gate> >/tmp/gate.log 2>&1`) so the reported status is make's own, then
read the file. If a tool may still be writing, hash `git diff` twice a few
seconds apart — differing hashes mean a straggler is mid-write.

**RECURRED AGAIN 2026-08-12, through the redirect.** The pipe is not the only
way to lose the status — **any** trailing command is. This ran as a background
Bash and notified `exit code 0`:

```sh
make pre-pr-remote > gate.log 2>&1; echo "MAKE_EXIT=$?"    # ← WRONG
```

`echo` is the last command in the list, so the *list's* status is echo's 0. The
`$?` text landed inside the terminal output, not in the harness's exit code, and
`gate.log` actually ended `make: *** [pre-pr-remote] Error 1`. Same false green,
no pipe involved.

Correct shape when a background task's exit code must be trustworthy — capture,
then re-raise it as the script's own status:

```sh
make pre-pr-remote > gate.log 2>&1
MAKE_EXIT=$?
echo "MAKE_EXIT=$MAKE_EXIT" >> gate.log
exit $MAKE_EXIT
```

Generalised rule: **the harness reports the exit status of the last thing the
command line runs.** A pipe, a `;`, an `&&` chain ending in `echo`, a trailing
`tail` — all discard it. Either make the gate the final command, or explicitly
`exit $MAKE_EXIT`. And regardless, still read the log: the status is one witness,
the output is the other.

The tell that saved it: the post-fixer `git diff --stat` was byte-identical to the pre-fixer
one. **A fixer pass that changed nothing is far more likely to have not run than to have
found nothing.** Related: [[feedback_verify_the_mutation_applied]],
[[reference_review_harness_claude_needs_foreground]], [[feedback_test_output_in_prod_log_faked_an_incident]]

---
name: reference-depot-attestation-is-vacuous-for-submodule-pointer-prs
description: "`make pre-pr-remote` cannot validate an owletto pointer bump — the patch injector skips the index, so all 18 lanes test the OLD pin and report green"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 90d4e325-62fd-4c7c-a94f-fe56982ad059
  modified: 2026-08-12T19:19:58.903Z
---

For a **submodule-pointer PR** the Depot tree attestation is real but **vacuous**:
the 18 lanes assemble a tree that does not contain the change, and pass.

**Mechanism.** Depot's injector applies the local diff with
`git apply --allow-empty /tmp/local.patch` and **no `--index`**. A gitlink lives
in the *index*, not the working tree, so the pointer change is silently dropped
(the patch is ~261 bytes and the runner still logs `Patch applied successfully`).
`.depot/actions/setup-submodule/action.yml` then runs
`git submodule update --init --recursive packages/owletto`, which **reads the
index** — so it checks out the BASE commit's pin. Observed on a bump run:
`Submodule path 'packages/owletto': checked out '6396cb92…'` — the old pin.

Ordering is not the cause; the patch step runs before the submodule step.

**How to apply:** on a pointer PR, the Depot green is the WEAK signal, inverted
from every other PR. The validation that means anything is GitHub CI on the
pushed branch, where `actions/checkout` with submodules resolves the real pin —
`frontend`, `check-drift`, `ui-review`. Never merge a pointer bump on the Depot
attestation alone.

**Not affected:** a branch that carries no gitlink diff
(`git diff origin/main...HEAD -- packages/owletto` empty). Its runners check out
the base pin, which is the correct one. Check this before assuming exposure.

Family: a check whose pass does not cover what you changed — see
[[reference-rebasing-a-gated-pr-costs-three-reruns]] and the stale-green
variant in [[feedback-compact-pr-status-and-ci-logs]]. Worse than stale-green:
that tested something true once; this tests the wrong tree by construction.

Provenance: injector flags reported by a peer session from its run log;
the `submodule update --init` half verified directly in
`.depot/actions/setup-submodule/action.yml`.

# Tools
